title: Browns need to ‘spread the help’ versus the Steelers in Week 4
summary: The Cleveland Browns are 2-1 heading into a big Thursday Night Football matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where the home team is the underdog. Despite the Browns strong start and playoff contention early in the season, Cleveland’s offensive line has not performed well. Whether it is PFF grades, earning Frownies, or just the overall film, […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns are 2-1 heading into a big Thursday Night Football matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where the home team is the underdog . Despite the Browns strong start and playoff contention early in the season , Cleveland’s offensive line has not performed well. Whether it is PFF grades , earning Frownies , or just the overall film, very few are lauding the unit upfront. The line was also not one of the reasons mentioned by fans for why the team is 2-1: The line’s concerns only grow if center Elgton Jenkins cannot play on Thursday . This offseason, OL Spencer Fano was considered the capstone of the new and improved Browns offensive line. The first offensive lineman selected in the 2026 NFL draft, Fano has not played poorly but, as noted in takeaways from Week 3 , Cleveland’s offense has done him no favors: Rookie Spencer Fano put on an island; looked like a rookie much of the game. Cleveland’s offense didn’t give him a lot of help and expected him to hold up. Unfortunately, it looks like film from the first two games showed that Fano could be beaten inside because Carolina attacked him there a lot. This analysis was backed up by former Browns and Ohio State Buckeyes star LeCharles Bentley a day later : I wish the Browns spread the help in pass protection a bit better. It’s a tall ask for a rookie left tackle to be on an island. In his Substack article, Bentley showed a video where Cleveland slid protection to the right, with five blockers for just three Panthers defenders. That not only left Fano blocking one-on-one, but also gave his defender a much larger area for his defender to attack. Instead of having a left guard and another defender directly to Fano’s right, Zion Johnson is blocking no one between the center and right guard: This is not a mistake by Johnson; instead, it was the protection call by the offense. Against an aggressive, veteran, and versatile Steelers defense, the Browns need to heed Bentley’s desire to “spread the help in pass protection” in Week 4. Otherwise, Deshaun Watson may not have a chance to get the offense going. How do you feel like Fano has played so far as a rookie? title: Browns big concern going into Week 4 vs. Steelers on Thursday Night Football
summary: The Cleveland Browns began Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season with five new starting offensive linemen. In the history of the league, that has never happened before. The Browns did not offer new deals to four of the five departing offensive linemen and waited to see if LG Joel Bitonio was coming back. This […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns began Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season with five new starting offensive linemen. In the history of the league, that has never happened before. The Browns did not offer new deals to four of the five departing offensive linemen and waited to see if LG Joel Bitonio was coming back. This meant starting over and building something new. RELATED: WEEK 4 INJURY REPORT One of the new offensive linemen signed during free agency was C/OG Elgton Jenkins from the Green Bay Packers . In college, he was named First Team All-American and a two-time SEC Academic Honor Roll recipient. So, he’s smart, which is a condition for playing center because this position must read the defensive front, identify who the middle linebacker is on each play, and indicate to his linemates potential blitzers. #Browns starting center Elgton Jenkins in the concussion protocol and might have to miss the #Steelers game Thurs night; Tytus Howard's 3 false starts 'not okay': Takeaways –> https://t.co/GLBIEZAjp7 — Mary Kay Cabot (@MaryKayCabot) September 28, 2026 Jenkins came out of training camp as the starting center and has played every snap in this position this year. Yet, he is now listed on the Browns injury report with a concussion. Which is odd, because he played every down in the victory over the Carolina Panthers. It’s unclear when the concussion first occurred, when it was diagnosed, and why he was allowed to continue to play until the final gun. What could have happened is that while in the locker room, somebody noticed something wasn’t right with him or he woke up Monday morning feeling off. Next is a focused neurological exam, balance test, and memory evaluation. If diagnosed with a concussion, the player enters the official Return-to-Participation Protocol. This becomes a five-step process without any set time limit and is then cleared by the team doctor. Next, he is evaluated by an independent neurological consultant before the athlete can be cleared for play. What is known, however, is that he is on the injury report and there is a good possibility that Jenkins will not play against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday Night Football. Monday injury report for #Browns and #Steelers , although neither practiced so projected. Concussion for center Elgton Jenkins and knee for Tylan Wallace. Austin Barber and Spencer Fano aren’t listed. pic.twitter.com/BXiM3CnHq8 — Chris Easterling (@ceasterlingABJ) September 28, 2026 Which is a huge problem. The center is the quarterback of the offensive line. It is Jenkins’ job to yell out protection calls and read the defensive front pre-snap so the rest of the linemen know who to block. He has the experience and has gelled nicely with his new linemates. It is a special position with special duties besides blocking on his own. And now, that line leader will be missing. In his stead will be either Luke Wypler or rookie Parker Brailsford, who was taken in the fifth round in this year’s NFL Draft. Both had plenty of success at the college level at the center position. Wypler played well last year during the few games he started in. He’s was also really good in pass blocking last year especially during Bills and Steelers game last year. — Liam Scoops Mcilwee (@LiamScoops) September 28, 2026 Wypler is the best bet since he is now in his fourth NFL season and has played in 25 games with six starts, including subbing for C Ethan Pocic in the final five games last season. He played every snap against the Chicago Bears, Buffalo Bills, and Steelers in Weeks 14 through 16 and then 67.3% of the time in the finale versus the Cincinnati Bengals. He appeared in every game last season, plus all three contests this year. However, he has had zero offensive snaps this season. Brailsford was a high school standout and was named First Team Arizona 5A All-State and a state champion in football. He has a history of being prepared in the game and also in life. It’s what most centers are made of. His feet never stop moving, and he is able to handle twist moves and delayed blitzes. Although he had a terrific camp and was mentioned by several media outlets as perhaps the best center, he doesn’t have any actual NFL game experience. Brailsford has been listed as inactive in each of the three contests so far. Which means he hasn’t been able to line up on special teams coverage teams or block on punts and field goals. He hasn’t tasted anything related to a real game. If Wypler is the new center, certainly the coaching staff will activate Brailsford as his backup for the Pittsburgh game. Regardless, losing Jenkins will become a huge hole. This offensive line has come a very long way and is just getting to form some consistency and build a cohesive unit. Now, this. Plus, Jenkins has really melded with QB Deshaun Watson in this new offense. Because of the short turnaround from Sunday’s game to the Thursday night event, the Browns practiced a walkthrough on Monday, and Jenkins was listed as DNP (did not participate). The protocol parameters are pretty stiff in the NFL. It will be almost impossible for Jenkins to clear the mandatory concussion protocol in time. title: Browns TE Harold Fannin Jr. continues on a strong trajectory
summary: Harold Fannin Jr. has been an important player to watch on the Cleveland Browns’ offense to start the season, and his impressive performance streak continued against the Carolina Panthers. In the Browns’ 21-18 win over the Panthers, Fannin Jr. recorded seven receptions for 51 yards and two touchdowns. It was another great showing that continued to show his role on […]
full_text: Harold Fannin Jr. has been an important player to watch on the Cleveland Browns’ offense to start the season, and his impressive performance streak continued against the Carolina Panthers. In the Browns’ 21-18 win over the Panthers, Fannin Jr. recorded seven receptions for 51 yards and two touchdowns. It was another great showing that continued to show his role on this Cleveland offense. One of Fannin Jr.’s touchdowns came during a crucial fourth-quarter drive, further showing that the moment is never too big for him. He contributed when it mattered most. It is highly likely that the Browns will find themselves in similar situations throughout the rest of the season. There will be close games and moments where the offense has to find a way to make a play. Fannin Jr. establishing himself as a reliable tight end and pass catcher could be the difference in some of these one-score games. After a rookie season where he had 72 receptions, 731 yards, and six touchdowns, all team highs, Fannin saw additions to the Browns passing game in KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston . The second-year tight end may not get over 100 targets this year, but his value to the team will continue to rise, as we saw in Week 3. It is still very early in the season, and there is a lot of football left to be played, so Fannin’s contributions could definitely change. These early weeks have been very promising, though, for the connection between him and quarterback Deshaun Watson . title: Browns Mason Graham is having a Pro Bowl year
summary: When the Cleveland Browns selected defensive tackle Mason Graham with the fifth overall pick in the first round of last year’s NFL draft, they envisioned pairing him with 2024 second-round pick DT Mike Hall for a formidable middle wall along the defensive front.   So far, only one of these two athletes is working out: […]
full_text: When the Cleveland Browns selected defensive tackle Mason Graham with the fifth overall pick in the first round of last year’s NFL draft, they envisioned pairing him with 2024 second-round pick DT Mike Hall for a formidable middle wall along the defensive front. So far, only one of these two athletes is working out: Graham. In just a three-game sample size, Graham has Pro Bowl written all over him. He is just the second Cleveland defensive player since Myles Garrett to record a sack in his first three games of any season. And he is accomplishing this from the interior of the line. RELATED: 2025 WINNING CARRIED OVER Graham already has four sacks in this young season. Cleveland has only played three games, which calculates to 1.33 sacks per contest. In a 17-game season, that would end up being 22.1 sacks for the year. From the inside. love to see the growth from Mason! @canadadry | #DawgPound pic.twitter.com/c3dAuOtBD4 — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) September 27, 2026 Keep in mind, Graham isn’t an EDGE rusher, but a defensive tackle. Normally, DTs are run stoppers and gap fillers, not pass rushers. Normally their sacks occur when the quarterback attempts to escape the pocket and run into the DT. But when DT Aaron Donald was in his prime, he demonstrated that defensive tackles can become productive and consistent pocket disruptors. pic.twitter.com/f9ooJZzJdC — Mistake by the Lake (@CLEBrownsfan84) September 28, 2026 Graham is doing the dirty work with excellent footwork and has a quick first step off the snap. This was demonstrated in this weekend’s victory over the Carolina Panthers. The Browns led by three late in the contest and wanted to drive the field for a game-tying field goal late in the fourth quarter. Carolina began their drive with 1:48 left in the game from their own 22. After an incomplete pass and a completion for no gain, they faced a third-and-10 needing to drive the field. On the third-down snap, Graham hit the B gap before right guard Robert Hunt could square up. Graham is in a full-out pass rush and turned his back to Hunt. Now all the guard can do is try to push Graham to his right out of harm’s way, but the Browns defensive tackle was gaining inches and ended up sliding off Hunt and eventually met and bear-hugged quarterback Bryce Young for the sack. This forced the Panthers to attempt a fourth down, and now, very long. It just happened to be Graham’s second sack of the day, but none was more important than the one as time was winding down. This forced the Panthers to go for it on a fourth-and-16. An eight-yard pass completion didn’t come close to gaining a first down and getting into field goal range, and the Browns got the ball back. DAWGS defense clutched up 🔥 pic.twitter.com/czJmj0qvCZ — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) September 28, 2026 This wasn’t Graham’s first case in the game of setting Carolina back. They began their third drive of the day early in the second quarter, beginning at their own 16. After several intermediate completions and some good gains on the ground, the Panthers found themselves at Cleveland’s 43 facing a fourth-and-three. Young began in the shotgun. Immediately off the snap, Graham was met by offensive guard Corey Bullock and center Luke Fortner, who double-teamed him. Graham then disengaged and headed into the center of the field where Young had set up. Graham hit the jets and nailed Young, who was still surveying the field at the 44-yard line, for his first sack of the game. Cleveland was now in good field position and, after seven plays, kicked a field goal, which ended up being the difference in the game. Graham has also improved his run-stopping ability. Midway through the third quarter, he nailed RB Chuba Hubbard for a minimal gain that gave Carolina a third-and-seven. And early in the fourth quarter, he caught RB A.J. Dillon for a two-yard loss after the Panthers had driven to Cleveland’s 23-yard line. After an incompletion, Carolina’s long drive now became a field goal conversion instead of six points. Graham finished the Panthers game with the fourth-most total tackles (7). He had the most tackles for loss (3) and sacks (2), along with two QB hits and five pressures, according to Pro Football Focus . The Carolina game was a great defensive effort in that the Browns pressured Young on 63% of his dropbacks, the highest mark by any NFL defense this year (in a single game), as stated by Ben Linsey of SumerSports . Five Cleveland defenders generated at least five quarterback pressures in this game. And out of respect to the other defensive linemen, Graham has been the Browns’ top pocket-collapser through the first three games of the season. He is tied for third in solo tackles and leads the team in tackles for loss (6) and sacks (4). His first sack of the season was in the beatdown in Week 1 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Right after the two-minute warning before halftime, the Jaguars had a third-and-one at their own 33 when Graham broke through and tackled quarterback Trevor Lawrence. This forced a punt and ended a good drive. In this game, Graham had five total tackles with two tackles for loss and a QB hit. atta boy Mason!! #CLEvsTB on CBS pic.twitter.com/9vODYK4e0F — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) September 20, 2026 Against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 2, Graham sacked former Browns quarterback Baker Mayfield late in the second quarter on a third-and-15, which also forced a punt. Ever since Myles Garrett was traded to the Los Angeles Rams, this group hasn’t had a face for the defense. Can Graham become the new look of this Browns defense? #Browns DT Mason Graham through 3 games: • 4 sacks • 9 QB pressures • 11.5% pressure rate The No. 5 pick in the 2025 NFL Draft joins Myles Garrett as the only Browns players to record at least one sack in each of the first 3 games of a season. pic.twitter.com/2hnaM8Smoq — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 28, 2026 Denzel Ward is the experienced veteran with proven production and Pro Bowl hardware. Last year’s NFL “Rookie Defensive Player of the Year” LB Carson Schwesinger routinely has double-digit tackle numbers each week and has the pedigree. And defensive end Jared Verse was supposed to be this year’s big splash, yet has minimal production with no sacks and only one pressure. This defense has kept Jim Schwartz’s personality, aggressiveness, and production. Who will rise to represent this unit? Could that be Graham? title: Cleveland Browns news: A big week in Cleveland sports
summary: This is shaping up to be quite the week for two of Cleveland’s professional sports teams. On Thursday night, in front of a national television audience, the Cleveland Browns will host the Pittsburgh Steelers in a game where the winner will end Week 4 no worse than tied for first place in the AFC North […]
full_text: (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images This is shaping up to be quite the week for two of Cleveland’s professional sports teams. On Thursday night, in front of a national television audience, the Cleveland Browns will host the Pittsburgh Steelers in a game where the winner will end Week 4 no worse than tied for first place in the AFC North Division. It is probably not hyperbole to say that Thursday night will be the biggest Browns game to date since the Wild Card playoff loss to the Houston Texans in 2023. If the Browns win – and they have not lost to the Steelers at home in five years – it could set them up for a surprising season. Then on Saturday, the Cleveland Guardians will open up their American League Division Series against either the Chicago White Sox or the Houston Astros. That is no surprise, as the Guardians have won the AL Central Division three years running and have made the playoffs in eight of the last 11 seasons. What a time to be in Cleveland! OK, enough about what is to come later this week. Let’s get the day rolling with the latest edition of the Daily Dawg Chow. Dawgs By Nature Browns HC Todd Monken: Slew of penalties is ‘embarrassing’ (Thomas Moore) : The head coach is not happy, especially about the penalties from the offensive linemen. But what can he do to fix the issue? Browns Tyson Campbell injury update plus offensive starter likely to miss Week 4 vs Steelers (Jared Mueller) : You take the good, you take the bad, and sometimes you are left with the possibility of having to play a backup at a key position. Browns roster moves: Swap out cornerbacks, again, according to a report (Jared Mueller) : The roster churn in the NFL never takes a day off. Browns vs. Steelers odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup (Chris Pokorny) : The Browns are home underdogs to a team that has not won in Cleveland since Spencer Fano was in high school. Browns Week 4: Steelers’ 2 wins have come in completely different ways (Jared Mueller) : It’s the Steelers, so they can go pound rocks. Browns 2027 NFL draft: Another Rams loss muddies Week 3 draft positioning (Jared Mueller) : It is still too early to dream of a meltdown in Los Angeles … or is it? title: Cleveland’s defense finds groove with insane pressure rate: Browns defensive snap counts
summary: This is a game where you don’t judge how things went by the stat sheet alone. QB Bryce Young nearly threw for 300 yards, and RB Chubba Hubbard had 82 yards rushing. But, at halftime, both players were bottled up, and it should have been a shutout if it hadn’t been for a bogus roughing […]
full_text: This is a game where you don’t judge how things went by the stat sheet alone. QB Bryce Young nearly threw for 300 yards, and RB Chubba Hubbard had 82 yards rushing. But, at halftime, both players were bottled up, and it should have been a shutout if it hadn’t been for a bogus roughing the passer penalty. Then, in the second half, the defense held Carolina to field goals multiple times, despite being in undesirable situations. After the offense re-took the lead, they closed out the game not once, but twice. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on defense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 3 game against the Carolina Panthers. Defensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats DL Mason Graham 56 73% 4 tackles, 3 assists (7 combined). 2 sacks, 3 TFL, 2 QH. DL Maliek Collins 53 69% 3 assists (3 combined). 2 QH. DL Jared Verse 52 68% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 QH. DL Isaiah McGuire 43 56% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 sack, 2 TFL, 1 QH. DL Mike Hall 38 49% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). DL Derek Barnett 27 35% 1 tackle (1 combined). 1 QH, 1 pass defended. DL Sam Williams 22 29% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Adin Huntington 17 22% 1 assist (1 combined). What a day by the defensive line. I was encouraged by what I saw from DT Mason Graham last year, but the leap from year one to year two is legitimate. Through three games, he looks like the Browns’ best defender along with CB Denzel Ward , with the ability to take over games. He had two sacks this week and 7 combined tackles. He was PFF’s fourth-highest graded defender, but only because a lot of defenders graded well, with a 73.4. Browns pressured Bryce Young on 51.0% of dropbacks, their 3rd-highest in a game since 2024. Jared Verse had a team-high six pressures. Nine different Browns had multiple pressures. (via @NextGenStats ) — Andrew Siciliano (@AndrewSiciliano) September 28, 2026 Derek Barnett (75.6), Jared Verse (72.3), Isaiah McGuire (69.2), Mike Hall (68.2), and Maliek Collins (62.6) all had their best grades by PFF of the season, as the pressures were coming from everywhere. I think we’re quickly seeing the defense be more aggressive as games go on, and they are finding ways to allow Verse to impact the game and free up other people, even if it doesn’t lead to sacks for him. Linebacker Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats LB Carson Schwesinger 77 100% 1 tackle, 5 assists (6 combined). LB Quincy Williams 74 96% 5 tackles, 4 assists (9 combined). 1 TFL, 1 QH. Much like on offense I think something looks a tad off with Quinshon Judkins , the same looks true for Carson Schewesinger on the defensive side of the ball. It’s not that he’s a liability, it’s that he seems like ‘just another guy,’ which is a far cry from a year ago. However, several fans are questioning why PFF graded Schwesinger as low as they did. On the other hand, who lit a fire under Quincy Williams this week? He was all over the place, making sure tackles everywhere. He was the team’s highest-graded defender by PFF, grading out to a 77.5. Cornerback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats CB Denzel Ward 76 99% 3 tackles (3 combined). 1 pass defended. CB Mekhi Blackmon 76 99% 6 tackles, 2 assists (8 combined). 1 pass defended. CB Myles Harden 60 78% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 pass defended. CB Noah Igbinoghene 2 3% No stats registered. Denzel Ward remained steady, playing a role in the Panthers’ top receivers not even getting passes thrown their way. Mekhi Blackmon filled in for Tyson Campbell . It’s not an easy task, but the Panthers went after him often. He was one of the team’s lowest-graded defenders by PFF, grading out to a 45.0. Safety Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats S Grant Delpit 77 100% 2 tackles, 2 assists (4 combined). S Ronnie Hickman 77 100% 3 tackles, 5 assists (8 combined). 1 INT, 1 pass defended. S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren 20 26% 3 assists (3 combined). Ronnie Hickman responded with a better outing this week, notably having an open field tackle to deny a first down, and also securing the interception to seal the game (even if that was more of a gift turnover). Grant Delpit , on the other hand, actually received the lowest PFF grade with a 40.0. Emmanuel McNeil-Warren has been consistent with about a quarter of the snaps each week.
author: Chris Pokorny

title: Shield your eyes from Deshaun Watson’s PFF grade: Browns offensive snap counts
summary: It wasn’t the smoothest operation on offense by the Browns, but they did enough for the win. Some elements you’re seeing help in the two wins that weren’t a foregone conclusion a year ago: not turning the ball over, and connecting on field goals. Those things can eventually turn out to be the difference in […]
full_text: It wasn’t the smoothest operation on offense by the Browns, but they did enough for the win. Some elements you’re seeing help in the two wins that weren’t a foregone conclusion a year ago: not turning the ball over, and connecting on field goals. Those things can eventually turn out to be the difference in these close games, and QB Deshaun Watson has come thrown in big moments. Cleveland converted 5-of-15 (33%) of their third downs, but were out-gained 360 yards to 259 yards. The time of possession battle was pretty even, though, as Todd Monken has maintained an even pass-run balance these first several games. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on offense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 3 game against the Carolina Panthers. Quarterback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats QB Deshaun Watson 69 99% 16-of-30 (53.3%) for 144 yards, 2 TD. 11 carries, 45 yards (4.1 YPC). QB Shedeur Sanders 1 1% 1-of-1 (100%) for 0 yards. Overall, it was not a sharp day throwing the football for Deshaun Watson . He was not as accurate as he was last week, often letting the ball sail a bit. But, for the second week in a row, he helped lead a go-ahead touchdown drive in the fourth quarter. He has also done a better job navigating up into the pocket when running. Sacks do not seem like his fault any more, and he seems to be making fairly good decisions. Dare I say it, he looks like a competent game manager. I feel like that mental hurdle he couldn’t shake over the past few years has finally been shook, with the final hurdle being that he even heard some cheers from the home crowd. PFF graded him with a 42.9, the lowest grade on offense. Despite the comeback, I think that’s fair, but it’s also a game where you use some discretion for what he did do well. Running Back Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats RB Quinshon Judkins 36 51% 18 carries, 70 yards (3.9 YPC). 2 catches, 9 yards (2 targets). RB Raheim Sanders 30 43% 1 carry, 17 yards (17.0 YPC). 4 catches, 34 yards (5 targets). FB Michael Burton 15 21% 0 catches (1 target). RB Jaleel McLaughlin 4 6% No stats registered. It may not have been the complete breakdown day I was hoping for, but Quinshon Judkins got a decent workload and averaged 3.9 YPC. Something still seems missing with Judkins right now. He looks very pedestrian or average. I don’t know if that’s a byproduct of the whole operation struggling. In terms of snap counts, Raheim Sanders saw the highest percentage of snaps for the backup running back this season. Judkins played 51% of the snaps, while Sanders was in for 43%. I think Sanders has done an admirable job as the backup, including as a receiver. He was the team’s third-highest graded player on offense this week by PFF, grading out to a 68.3. Wide Receiver Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats WR Denzel Boston 62 89% 2 catches, 41 yards (4 targets). WR KC Concepcion 60 86% 2 catches, 9 yards (9 targets). WR Jerry Jeudy 36 51% No stats registered. WR Tylan Wallace 14 20% No stats registered. WR Isaiah Bond 5 7% No stats registered. WR Malachi Corley 1 1% No stats registered. It’s no longer a fluke: for the second week in a row, Jerry Jeudy was third among the receivers, and had his snap count percentage dip to 51%. He did draw one pass interference penalty that doesn’t show up in the stat sheet above, but otherwise was not targeted again. Denzel Boston only had 2 catches, but they were big ones again, and he was the team’s highest-graded player by PFF, grading out to a 73.8. This wasn’t a breakout game for KC Concepcion , who had 2 catches for 9 yards on 9 targets . Now, much of those incompletions seemed like Watson struggling to connect with him, as opposed to Concepcion being at fault. The team wasn’t able to utilize him on any jet sweeps or creative plays this week. The offense in general might need to continue boosting its stock all around, to reduce defenses from keying in so much on him at times. PFF broke down the WR lineups a little more: Denzel Boston has been the Browns’ X receiver all season, playing over 90% of snaps in 11 and 12 personnel and the majority of 13 personnel snaps, giving him a 91.1% snap rate on the season. Concepcion held a slight lead over Jeudy for the second spot over the first two weeks. Concepcion played 85.5% of snaps in 11 personnel, but only 42.4% in 12 personnel. Jeudy was playing 54.5% in 12 personnel, but only 69.6% in 11, losing some snaps primarily to Tylan Wallace. This rotation left Concepcion at a 67% snap rate and Jeudy at 60.6%. Tight End Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats TE Harold Fannin 60 86% 7 catches, 51 yards (9 targets), 2 TD. TE Blake Whiteheart 27 39% No stats registered. For two straight weeks, Harold Fannin has been a big factor in the passing game. He continued to break some tackles this week, and then in the red zone, got away from defenders as he crossed the field for two touchdown catches. Fannin was the team’s second-highest graded player on offense by PFF, grading out to a 69.2. Offensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats OL Spencer Fano 70 100% OL Zion Johnson 70 100% OL Elgton Jenkins 70 100% OL Austin Barber 70 100% OL Tytus Howard 70 100% After rookie Austin Barber thrived in a couple games, he struggled against the Panthers. His pass blocking grade by PFF was the lowest among the offensive linemen (42.7). Fellow rookie Spencer Fano also graded low in pass blocking (50.8), although he at least was the team’s highest-graded run blocker (77.2). Tytus Howard was dinged for three false starts, but in terms of PFF blocking grades, he probably had the most complete performance. C Elgton Jenkins — who is now in the concussion protocol — was the team’s best-graded pass blocker (80.2).

title: Browns HC Todd Monken: Slew of penalties is ‘embarrassing’
summary: The Cleveland Browns, perhaps more than other NFL teams, consistently struggle with overcoming their own mistakes, especially when the offense has the ball. It has played out time and time again – the offense gets a little bit of momentum, a penalty (be it a false start, illegal formation, or holding call) is called, and […]
full_text: (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns, perhaps more than other NFL teams, consistently struggle with overcoming their own mistakes, especially when the offense has the ball. It has played out time and time again – the offense gets a little bit of momentum, a penalty (be it a false start, illegal formation, or holding call) is called, and the drive fizzles out. Fans and media rejoiced in the offseason when the Browns hired Todd Monken as head coach because he was the type of “old-school head coach” who was finally going to “lay down the law” and hold these lazy players accountable after so many years of lax treatment. Or so the story went until the season began. Week 1 against Jacksonville saw the Browns commit 11 penalties, then six more in Week 2 against Tampa Bay. The situation reached an absurd level on Sunday against Carolina as the Browns were penalized 12 times, including five on the offensive line in one series alone: An illegal formation on right tackle Tytus Howard A false start on right guard Austin Barber A false start on Howard A holding call on left tackle Spencer Fano A false start on Howard In the words of the legendary Green Bay head coach Vince Lombardi, “What the hell is going on out there?” It is a good question, and an important one to answer if the Browns hope to keep the momentum of their current two-game winning streak going on Thursday night against the Pittsburgh Steelers. The offense is simply not good enough yet to overcome so many penalties, so what is the answer? More time on task in practice? Better mental focus from the players? Better coaching? Monken was asked about the situation on Monday, and his answer was “all of the above” : “Coaching and playing alike, mental stamina with shifts and motions, getting aligned properly, proper snap count. It’s all of the above. It’s hard when it doesn’t show up in practice. When it doesn’t show up in practice, it’s hard to wrap your head around why we had the issues that we did. But it’s got to be fixed. It’s got to be fixed in a hurry with a short week.” All the penalties were problematic, but the false starts were particularly egregious, given that the Browns were playing at home and crowd noise wasn’t an issue. For what it’s worth, Monken was not making any excuses on Monday : “That’s embarrassing. We got to get it fixed in a hurry. It’s shitty football, I mean, it is what it is. You’ve heard me say it before, and that’s coaching and playing. And again, we had not seen that. You get one thing semi-fixed with your operation and get into the line of scrimmage, and then this comes up, and it’s Browns hurting Browns, and we know it. And now we’re going to work like hell to get it fixed.” "Why are you jumping offside? Why are you going early? I mean, that's not on coaching. That's on the players." #DawgPound @HanfordDixon29 needs more from Tytus Howard and the o-line. pic.twitter.com/aWZ8SOkwrs — BIGPLAY Cleveland (@BIGPLAYcle) September 28, 2026 Of the starters on the offensive line, Howard is struggling the most, with five penalties and the lowest Pro Football Focus grade (50.3) among the starters , which has not gone unnoticed by Monken : “If you’re trying to anticipate the snap count, and I told Tytus this today, it’s like a defensive lineman trying to anticipate the snap count. And if you jump offsides, you false start once, OK, right, like, all right, I get it. After that, it’s over. It’s not OK. It’s not kosher anymore. So that’s on him. He knows it, and we’ve got to get it cleaned up.” With only one day of practice before the game against the Steelers, it seems unlikely that Monken will make a change, but if Howard struggles again on Thursday night, it could be time to give Dawand Jones a chance at right tackle in Week 5 against the New York Jets. Other than that, there’s not much else Monken can do other than have the players work it out while throwing in some of that “old-school coaching” that got people so excited about when he was first hired. title: Browns Tyson Campbell injury update plus offensive starter likely to miss Week 4 vs Steelers
summary: The Cleveland Browns head into the short week versus the Pittsburgh Steelers with a chance to take over the top spot in the AFC North. Thursday Night Football can often lead to teams playing it safe with their injured players and walkthroughs more than practices. Early in the season, the Browns have mostly had good […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns head into the short week versus the Pittsburgh Steelers with a chance to take over the top spot in the AFC North . Thursday Night Football can often lead to teams playing it safe with their injured players and walkthroughs more than practices. Early in the season, the Browns have mostly had good injury luck, but CB Tyson Campbell missing Week 3 was concerning . Heading into Week 4, Cleveland HC Todd Monken noted that Campbell was close to playing versus the Carolina Panthers and was likely to play against the Steelers this week. Neither team practiced on Monday, but were required to create participation/injury reports for Week 4 based on their estimates of what players would have been able to do. Browns injury report CB Tyson Campbell – Knee – Limited S Grant Delpit – Shoulder – Limited OL Tytus Howard – Knee – Limited OL Elgton Jenkins – Concussion – DNP OL Teven Jenkins – Back – DNP WR Tylan Wallace – Knee – DNP E. Jenkins is likely to miss Thursday Night Football due to the testing requirements for the concussion protocol. Rookie Paker Brailsford is listed as the backup center, but he’s been inactive to start the season, while Luke Wypler has been active. Steelers injury report CB Jalen Ramsey – Wrist – Limited RB Rico Dowdle – Toe – DNP CB Joey Porter Jr. – Not injury related/conditioning – Full CB Brandin Echols – Concussion – Limited Porter has not played in Pittsburgh’s first three games due to a contract dispute and returning from a back issue in training camp. It seems unlikely, based on the Steelers’ rules against negotiating in season, that Porter will return for this week’s contest. How big of a deal do you think E. Jenkins’ injury would be if he has to miss the game? Do you think Porter plays this week? Join the conversation! title: Browns roster moves: Swap out cornerbacks, again, according to a report
summary: Could I just copy and paste Chris’ report from last week and swap out the cornerback names? Pretty much. Will I? Not in totality. The Cleveland Browns, coming off a big win in Week 3 and looking forward to Week 4’s Thursday Night Football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, will be doing things in a […]
full_text: Could I just copy and paste Chris’ report from last week and swap out the cornerback names ? Pretty much. Will I? Not in totality. The Cleveland Browns, coming off a big win in Week 3 and looking forward to Week 4’s Thursday Night Football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers , will be doing things in a condensed fashion this week. As always with GM Andrew Berry, the bottom of the roster and the practice squad continue to see changes on a regular basis. Last Wednesday, the Browns signed CB D’Angelo Ross to the practice squad and released CB Myles Bryant . Ross was not elevated for Sunday’s contest and, reportedly, Bryant will return to the practice squad and Ross will depart: The Browns signed CB Myles Bryant back to the practice squad and released CB D’Angelo Ross from the practice squad, per the NFL transaction wire. — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 28, 2026 Ross was signed by the Browns last November and played in some regular season games. He competed for a roster spot this camp, but began the season on the practice squad. He was a practice squad elevation in Week 1, before being released on September 15. Bryant is in his seventh year in the NFL, having played in 77 games combined with the New England Patriots and the Houston Texans. Bryant signed with the Browns as a free agent in April, but has yet to play a game for the team. Cleveland has not made the move official, nor has their roster been adjusted online despite multiple reports of the move being on the NFL’s transaction wire.

title: Cowboys vs Ravens: Brian Schottenheimer leads a disaster-class loss
summary: There are losses that happen because the other team is simply better. Then there are losses where a team spends the final few minutes handing its opponent every opportunity to survive. Sunday’s 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in Brazil felt like the latter. The Cowboys had the ball at the Baltimore two-yard line with […]
full_text: REUTERS/Brian Snyder | REUTERS There are losses that happen because the other team is simply better. Then there are losses where a team spends the final few minutes handing its opponent every opportunity to survive. Sunday’s 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in Brazil felt like the latter. The Cowboys had the ball at the Baltimore two-yard line with 23 seconds remaining, a timeout in their pocket and a chance to take the lead. They didn’t score a touchdown. 23 seconds later, the Ravens were celebrating after Tyler Loop drilled a 56-yard field goal at the gun. Plenty went wrong before those final 23 seconds, however. Dallas committed seven penalties for 88 yards, went just 3-for-5 in the red zone and repeatedly found ways to turn promising situations into field goals or empty possessions. Even head coach Brian Schottenheimer admitted afterward that some of the biggest mistakes were his. Asked to grade his performance as a play-caller, Schottenheimer gave himself an “F.” The Cowboys had plenty of opportunities It’s important to establish that Dallas did not get dominated Sunday. The Cowboys gained 415 yards to Baltimore’s 378, held the ball for 30:38 and produced 27 first downs. Dak Prescott threw for 276 yards, CeeDee Lamb had 112 receiving yards, and Javonte Williams ran for 98 yards as Dallas finally got its ground game moving. This was a winnable football game. That’s precisely why the bone-headed mistakes the Cowboys regularly make matter. Dallas’ first possession reached the Baltimore 1-yard line, but instead of handing the ball to Williams after he had a productive drive, the Cowboys called two straight passes. The first fell incomplete. The second resulted in a 9-yard sack. A drive that could have produced seven points produced three. Later, a holding penalty on Terence Steele wiped out a third-down conversion after a big George Pickens catch. The Cowboys eventually had the ensuing 59-yard field goal blocked, and Baltimore immediately drove for a touchdown. These weren’t impossible problems to overcome. They were the kinds of problems good teams don’t make. The play-calling The Cowboys’ tendency to get cute showed up multiple times . Notably, when Jake Ferguson caught a shovel pass that ended in a fumble, another promising possession went nowhere. Dallas had Prescott playing efficiently, Lamb making plays, Pickens contributing, and Williams running the football effectively. The offense didn’t need to reinvent the wheel every time it reached the red zone or found an opportunity to extend a drive. A coach has to understand his playbook, but a head coach also has to understand his personnel well enough to know when the situation calls for creativity and when it calls for trusting the players who have already established an advantage. On Sunday, Schottenheimer didn’t always seem to make that distinction. It seemed like he was hedging between not fully trusting the offense that was on the field and having to be the smartest guy on the sidelines. Overthinking, overcoaching, overreacting. Red-zone offense is still a huge question mark The Cowboys finished 3-for-5 in the red zone, and the two failures were costly because both came in situations where Dallas had a realistic opportunity to take control of the game. It felt like there were at least a dozen moments in this game where that could have happened, but pinpointing these two would-be opportunities highlights the shortcomings. The most consequential sequence came at the end of the game and Dallas at Baltimore’s 22-yard line. A pass interference penalty on Nate Wiggins moved the Cowboys to the two-yard line, giving Dallas first-and-goal with 23 seconds remaining and an opportunity to take the lead. ESPN’s win probability put Dallas at 77.5% at that point. Four downs and a timeout separated the Cowboys from a potential touchdown. Instead, Prescott threw an incomplete pass to Pickens on first down. Then Luke Schoomaker’s false start pushed the Cowboys back five yards. Prescott scrambled for two yards on the next play before throwing the ball away on third down, leaving Brandon Aubrey to attempt a 23-yard field goal with seven seconds remaining. Schottenheimer acknowledged that he had instructed Prescott to take the conservative approach on third down. “I probably over-coached Dak on that one, because we had the points,” Schottenheimer said. “It had to go to GP or throw it away. That’s on me. I over-coached him.” Prescott even admitted afterward that he probably should have held onto the ball longer and left it near the front pylon. That exchange tells you a lot about what went wrong. Schottenheimer was trying to eliminate the possibility of a negative play, but in doing so he also eliminated the opportunity to do what he is paid to do. Win the game. Rather than trusting his quarterback to make the best decision with the game on the line, Schotty attempted to script the outcome too tightly. That is not necessarily a problem on its own. But when combined with the earlier goal-line decisions, the shovel pass and the Cowboys’ repeated tendency to move away from what was working, it begins to look less like an isolated decision and more like a coach struggling to trust his own offense. Lack of urgency People typically mix urgency in football with speed and tempo. That isn’t wrong, but I think a coach like Schottenheimer fails to realize it also means not taking a play for granted. After Aubrey tied the game with seven seconds to go before overtime, the Cowboys avoided the risk of a long return by kicking the touchback, even though they could have burned valuable seconds off the clock. Now to the last offensive play. There is plenty to discuss about the defensive call on that final play, and that responsibility ultimately falls more directly on defensive coordinator Christian Parker. Schottenheimer explained afterward that he liked the defensive call because he wanted the Cowboys to remain aggressive and “sticky” in coverage, which they weren’t, giving up a 27-yard pass to a wide-open Zay Flowers. Tyler Loop then banged home the game-winner. As the head coach, Schottenheimer owns the larger sequence. The Cowboys had just tied the game with seven seconds remaining. Instead of forcing Baltimore to return the kick before attempting a desperation pass, Dallas kicked the ball into the end zone for a touchback, allowing the Ravens to start at their own 35-yard line with all seven seconds remaining. Jackson then needed only one completion to put Baltimore in range. The decision may have made sense within the defensive philosophy the Cowboys had in mind, but in practice and in hindsight, it was foolish. Still, the result was another example of a game where the Cowboys had a chance to control the situation and instead let the opponent dictate it. It really felt like the Cowboys thought the Ravens would just take this game into overtime. If they kept everything in front of them and didn’t give up a touchdown, they’d head to OT with a fresh start. They reckoned there was no way the Ravens would play to win. What now ? The Cowboys did not lose because their offense was incapable of moving the football, or because the defense couldn’t get stops; they had a few. They lost because the team repeatedly struggled to turn that production and those stops into the situational execution that closes games. Schottenheimer must figure out what his offense does best and trust it when the game demands it. If Williams is running effectively, Dallas needs to stay with him. If Lamb and Pickens are winning their matchups, stick with them. The offense should not feel compelled to manufacture something simply because the defense might be expecting the obvious answer. When Prescott has the ball with the game on the line, the coaching staff has to give him just the right amount of guidance to succeed without taking away the instincts that have made him one of the league’s more productive quarterbacks. Schottenheimer deserves credit for…

full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys are ailing on defense. It was reported on Monday that safety Jalen Thompson, one of the handful of players banged up in last week’s loss in Brazil, would miss a month or more, and Jerry Jones corroborated that on Tuesday morning during his appearance on 105.3 The Fan. title: Cowboys rookie report: Jaishawn Barham delivers big in Ravens loss
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ trip to Brazil ended in frustration, with the Baltimore Ravens winning on a last-second field goal. For the rookie class, there were reasons for encouragement. Caleb Downs helped create an early scoring opportunity, while Jaishawn Barham produced two second-half stops that gave Dallas a chance to take control. The challenge remains turning […]
full_text: Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys’ trip to Brazil ended in frustration, with the Baltimore Ravens winning on a last-second field goal. For the rookie class, there were reasons for encouragement. Caleb Downs helped create an early scoring opportunity, while Jaishawn Barham produced two second-half stops that gave Dallas a chance to take control. The challenge remains turning those individual moments into a complete defensive performance. But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. Caleb Downs (Defensive snaps: 64 | Tackles: 3 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0) Downs’ biggest contribution came early, stopping Derrick Henry for no gain on fourth-and-one and handing Dallas possession at Baltimore’s 30-yard line. That short field became an important Cowboys touchdown which added weight to Down’s stop. His tackle total was modest, but the importance of that stop was considerable. This was a game with a valuable individual highlight, alongside a couple of things to clean up. Malachi Lawrence (Defensive snaps: 17 | Tackles: 2 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 0 | Special-teams tackles: 1) Lawrence assisted on two defensive tackles and contributed a kickoff tackle, but his opportunities to rush Lamar Jackson were limited. He made only three pass-rush snaps, with no pressure generated. That small sample matters when judging the performance as Dallas needs more disruption from its edge defenders, but Lawrence had relatively few chances to provide it. His contribution was mainly supporting the run defense and covering kicks. Jaishawn Barham (Defensive snaps: 50 | Tackles: 7 | TFL: 2 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 1) Barham provided the strongest rookie performance, particularly when Dallas desperately needed a response. His fourth-and-goal stop against Henry denied Baltimore a touchdown, and another tackle behind the line on the following Ravens possession helped keep the Cowboys in the fight. Those were substantial plays against one of the league’s most difficult runners to bring down. Brian Schottenheimer also praised his command of the defense while handling the green-dot communication duties. There were mistakes alongside the highlights. Barham did make two missed tackles against the run and four completions for 50 yards in coverage. His response was the encouraging part. He continued making decisive plays rather than allowing the difficult moments to define his night. LT Overton (Defensive snaps: 15 | Tackles: 2 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 0) Overton’s limited appearance earned an encouraging initial PFF grade of 77.4. His contribution came against the run, but he generated no pressures on six pass-rush snaps. It was a promising small sample, with pass-rush production still to develop.

title: The Cowboys secondary has become depleted
summary: The defense of the Dallas Cowboys is struggling right now. Struggling to play well, but also struggling to stay healthy. The team is suffering from several injuries, but the defensive back group is being put through the wringer. Each week, a new player goes down, sometimes more than one, leaving the secondary gutted and the […]
full_text: Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images | Getty Images The defense of the Dallas Cowboys is struggling right now. Struggling to play well, but also struggling to stay healthy. The team is suffering from several injuries, but the defensive back group is being put through the wringer. Each week, a new player goes down, sometimes more than one, leaving the secondary gutted and the coaching staff reaching deep for answers. In a matter of three short weeks, this has turned into a crisis area for this football team. Let’s take a look at the casualties. As you can see, the secondary was down three players entering the Baltimore game and lost two more. That’s a total of five starters/key role players on the defense. This wave of injuries is hurtful to a Christian Parker defense because of how he uses his defensive backs. He’s heavily reliant on safeties, having three on the field a great majority of the time. But it’s not just the quantity, it’s the quality. He requires his safeties to be versatile so they can be used to disguise looks and provide late-snap rotations to sneakily switch coverage responsibilities, making it hard on opposing offenses. Having three stealthy safeties is out of the question now as Parker is just lucky if he has enough bodies to throw out on the field. Three of his top four safeties have gotten hurt, leaving rookie Caleb Downs as the team’s only quality safety left. And he plays a lot of time down in the box. The cornerback position is almost as bad. They lost Cobie Durant in Week 2 and then turned around and lost Shavon Revel Jr. on Sunday, leaving DaRon Bland as the only healthy starter available. With most of the top guys wiped out, the team is now in survival mode. Backup safeties Markquese Bell and Alijah Clark have taken on greater roles. Bell has some hybrid ability as a former linebacker, but he is not strong in coverage. He was flagged for that costly pass interference when the Ravens’ receiver had to come back for the underthrown deep ball. Clark is a core special teams player, but he played 20 snaps on defense on Sunday. At cornerback, the team will turn to Caelen Carson (17 snaps on Sunday), Ameer Speed (4), and Reddy Steward (2). Carson is a boundary corner who can be a little grabby at times. Speed also plays on the outside, while Steward is exclusively a slot corner, a position occupied by the rookie Downs. The recent injuries to Thompson and Revel Jr. bring a dark cloud over the secondary, especially with the uncertainty of their severity. Thompson is expected to miss at least a month. The knee hyperextension of Revel isn’t something you want to hear about, especially considering he is recovering from an ACL injury, but it’s not the same knee, so that’s good. We’ll have to keep our ears close to the ground as more updates become available. There is some good news as both Hooker and Durant could be returning real soon. Neither was placed on injured reserve, so their time missed wasn’t expected to be that long. If they were able to return this weekend against the Houston Texans, that would be impeccable timing. Also, the team will likely be scouring the waiver wire, looking for more depth pieces to add. The coaching staff will continue to make adjustments and look for the right guys to make this defense work. This is quite a challenge for a young defensive coordinator who already has his work cut out for him. Without the right guys to do the things he needs, it severely limits the dynamic of the defensive scheme. Things just go that much harder for the Cowboys defense.

title: Cowboys vs. Ravens Stock Report: Brian Schottenheimer failed the team
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are likely going to be thinking about that one for a while. Sunday’s loss to the Baltimore Ravens was as inconsequential as a game can get in terms of tiebreaker worth. Dallas lost to an AFC team and one that isn’t even a common opponent with their division rivals. If you had […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Rio De Janeiro, BRA; Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer looks on during the game against the Baltimore Ravens at Maracana Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys are likely going to be thinking about that one for a while. Sunday’s loss to the Baltimore Ravens was as inconsequential as a game can get in terms of tiebreaker worth. Dallas lost to an AFC team and one that isn’t even a common opponent with their division rivals. If you had ranked games before the season by which would be the “best” to lose then this would have been number one for those reasons. But while it isn’t a tiebreaker or measurable variable, the narrative matters. This was an opportunity for the Cowboys to prove that they could hang (which they did, to be clear) and maybe even beat (which they didn’t, also to be clear) one of the better teams in the NFL. It was the proverbial measuring stick game and the Cowboys did not measure up. That is reflected in our stock report following the loss to say the least. Stock Down: Brian Schottenheimer You can argue about different parts of the Cowboys letting them down on Sunday and have a fair point. The offense did not fully deliver, the defense certainly got beat in bad moments, and special teams were a disaster. But the biggest stock down here has to be Brian Schottenheimer. He is both the head coach who oversees the entire operation and the offensive play-caller who got way too cute for much of this game and handicapped things at the end. Schottenheimer’s hiring is now being called into question and it is hard to push back on any of those sorts of conversations. He was the most direct reason for the Cowboys’ loss on Sunday and directly inhibited the team’s chances of winning. Your head coach has to be your advantage in games and on Sunday he was the opposite. Stock Down: Brandon Aubrey Brandon Aubrey had a field goal attempt blocked which was obviously unfortunate, especially given that the Cowboys lost the game by three points. But that isn’t why he’s here. Aubrey had multiple kickoffs that went out of bounds and they became such an issue that the coaching staff didn’t trust him to keep the ball in bounds with seven seconds remaining . Aubrey booting it out of the endzone drew no time off of the clock and provided Baltimore with every second, literally, they needed to pull the win off. This past offseason the Cowboys made Aubrey the highest-paid kicker in the NFL. Aubrey reached a level of non-trust before the calendar even turned to October. This cannot happen. Stock Down: Jake Ferguson I’m hesitant to place Ferguson here given that his fumble was debatable, in terms of whether or not he had full possession before it happened, and that he had a critical touchdown during Dallas’ rally. But he had what the game defined to be as a fumble, and the narrative that he has a fumbling issue is only going to persist. His place is earned, unfortunately. Stock Down: Luke Schoonmaker Conversations around Schoonmaker are never pleasant as most Cowboys fans have felt like he has under-delivered on his second-round draft status. He is not an offensive weapon for this team which is disappointing. But you can not be an offensive weapon and still be helpful. At the very least you can not be an offensive weapon and not cost your team. This was not the case for Schoonmaker on Sunday. His false start penalty was one of the bigger butterfly effect moments from the game as it dramatically changed what Dallas was able to do as they were trying to win the game. Those mistakes add up. Stock Down: Ryan Flournoy By extension, you could lump Dak Prescott in here too as he is the one playing quarterback, but consider that Ryan Flournoy had eight total targets in this game. He had two receptions. The Cowboys paid Flournoy, not CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens money to be sure, but still. We have all raved about him as one of the better WR3s in the NFL. He has to do more with that many targets. Stock Down: Terence Steele At a certain point enough is enough. It isn’t 100% Steele’s fault. We have all known for a while that he is among the weakest points on the team overall, but the Cowboys were painted into a bit of a corner this past offseason. They had questions about Tyler Guyton, more on him in a moment, and couldn’t quite trust him. As a result they weren’t able to also move on from Steele. They had to hedge themselves however they could. Unfortunately, Steele hasn’t seen the improvement this year that the other player we are talking about has. Enough definitely feels like enough. Sunday did not go well. Stock Up: Jaishawn Barham What a phenomenal performance. Consider that the Cowboys had an answer in this game for Derrick Henry. Think about how absurd that is. Now obviously they didn’t fully neutralize Henry, but they took care of him when the moments mattered the most. Jaishawn Barham helped do that. If there is one bright light to shine through Sunday’s darkness it is that the Cowboys really do appear to have something special in Barham. Stock Up: Tyler Guyton NextGenStats counted 44 total pass snaps that Tyler Guyton was charged to protect Dak Prescott on, and he did so on 40 of them. Literally. Guyton allowed, as NGS evaluated, just four pressures in this game, all of them to Trey Hendrickson. He has really found himself. Stock Up: CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens Dak Prescott had 25 completions in this game. 14 of them went to CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. The reason this matters is that Prescott was 14 of 19 when targeting these two specifically. He was 11 of 21 when targeting everyone else. Maybe throw it to Lamb and Pickens more? Just an idea! Obviously there is some jest in that, but the point is that Lamb and Pickens are proving week in and week out that they are very much worth the hype around them. There is an argument to spreading the wealth, so to speak, but it is clear that this is where the money is made for this team. Stock Up: Quinnen Williams Barham was the star on defense, but this was one of Quinnen Williams’ better games with the Cowboys. It was particularly great to see after the first two weeks of the season were hardly his best. Williams was a serious force early on, but obviously everybody wore down as the game wore on. That is to be expected on some level, but at the very least Williams did his job to position other players like Barham to succeed.

title: Cowboys vs. Ravens: The good, the bad, and the ugly from Week 3
summary: The Dallas Cowboys 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens Sunday afternoon in Brazil is a game chocked full of “what could’ve been”. The Cowboys had the game within their grasp, but unfortunately shot themselves in the foot in the end allowing the Ravens to steal the victory with a last second field goal. C’est la […]
full_text: Photo by Wagner Meier/Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens Sunday afternoon in Brazil is a game chocked full of “what could’ve been”. The Cowboys had the game within their grasp, but unfortunately shot themselves in the foot in the end allowing the Ravens to steal the victory with a last second field goal. C’est la vie. Last week’s loss in the past and there’s nothing we can do to change the outcome. It’s now time to shift the focus to Dallas’ next opponent, Houston Texans. Before we do that though, let’s was take one last look back at some of the good, bad, and ugly things that occurred that led to their unfortunate loss to Baltimore. THE GOOD – RB Javonte Williams Who would’ve guessed Javonte Williams would out rush Derrick Henry? That’s exactly what he did though. He averaged 5.2 yards per carry on 19 carries and rushed for a total of 98 yards and a touchdown Sunday afternoon against Baltimore. After rushing for just 30 and 41 yards in his first two games this year, this was a much-needed addition the Cowboys offense, especially against a stout Ravens run defense. Unfortunately it wasn’t enough to secure the “W”, but it was a positive sign Dallas’ offense is finally started a fire on all cylinders. THE BAD – HC Brian Schottenheimer There are several things that occurred throughout the ballgame Sunday afternoon that ultimately led to the Cowboys loss, but quite a bit of it can be laid at the feet of Brian Schottenheimer. From his questionable play-calling in the red zone to his in-game decision-making, he had a negative impact on the outcome of the game. The choice to kick the ball out of the endzone and not run any time off the clock really came back to hurt the team. Schottenheimer has done plenty of good things with the Cowboys, but this game was not his best moment. THE UGLY – Injuries The Cowboys continued to take a hit at the safety position and cornerback. Jalen Thompson now joins Malik Hooker and P.J. Locke as latest injured safety, leaving Dallas with a couple of backups starting for them for the foreseeable future. Locke is probably out until at least after Week 7 after being placed on injured reserve and there is no timetable for Thompson or Hooker to return to action. Both could be out for at least a couple more weeks. Shavon Revel had to leave the Ravens game, joining fellow cornerback Cobie Durant on the injured list. This led to the Cowboys playing with backups deep off their bench, helping the late-game collapse. The Cowboys secondary has been decimated by injury.
author: Brian Martin

title: Cowboys can’t win with coaching and other mistakes costing them
summary: “Football” fans in Rio de Janiero, Brazil are certainly used to games coming down to exciting kicks. When it came to the American football game between the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens played there on Sunday, the home team Cowboys will be regretting opportunities to win it before it ever came down to Tyler Loop’s […]
full_text: Photo by Wagner Meier/Getty Images | Getty Images “Football” fans in Rio de Janiero, Brazil are certainly used to games coming down to exciting kicks. When it came to the American football game between the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens played there on Sunday, the home team Cowboys will be regretting opportunities to win it before it ever came down to Tyler Loop’s 56-yard field goal on the last snap of the game. We say all the time that games must be won and lost in the NFL with your best players on the field, and the Cowboys had a golden opportunity to do so with Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and George Pickens moving the offense downfield for a 1st-and-goal at the two-yard line with 23 seconds left, down by three. A Dallas team that previously led 10-0 in the first quarter but needed to rally back from trailing Baltimore 24-13 late in the third quarter, failed to win the game with their self-proclaimed “greatest offense there is” poised to do so from the goal line. They did manage to leave just seven seconds for the Ravens to work with in a tie game. Lamar Jackson and Zay Flowers took that seven seconds against a Cowboys defense down to backup players in the secondary, and set up the winning field goal. Jackson had a clean pocket to hit Flowers for a 27-yard gain down the middle with one second left to call a timeout, and out trotted Loop to break the heart of Cowboys nation. The Cowboys are now 1-2 for the third season in a row, and will prepare for an in-state battle against the Houston Texans, who also have some soul-searching to do after falling to 0-3 on Sunday as well. Let’s get to some notes on a wild back-and-forth affair between the Cowboys and Ravens in Brazil. In our weekly look at what the Cowboys most needed to do to win this game, we put the focus on the interior defensive line needing to finally step up, as well as the offensive line getting movement in the run game. Like literally everything in this loss, there were good and bad things that flipped and flopped back and forth for 60 minutes. Quinnen Williams asserted himself into the game on the very first drive by pressuring Jackson right in his face, forcing a sailed pass beyond Mark Andrews’ reach, despite him being wide open. Unfortunately, the relationship between these splash plays up front and how they correlated to a depleted Cowboys secondary being able to hold up enough did not translate enough for a win. The glaring missing piece was a consistent threat off the edge to support a strong effort from the interior defenders up front, and in particular Rashan Gary really struggled. Dallas lost the big-play differential thanks in large part to being gashed way too much in the secondary. For much of the afternoon, chunk plays came almost effortlessly for the Ravens, while the Cowboys had a hard time pushing the ball downfield. The Cowboys should have came away with more points early as they got downfield with Javonte Williams getting loose the best he had all season. An incomplete play-action pass on 2nd-and-goal killed the momentum of the drive followed by a third-down sack and the team had to settle for three. There were other instances of the defense rising to the occasion situationally that shouldn’t be completely forgotten about. Quinnen Williams again had penetration that led to a Jaishawn Barham tackle for loss on the Ravens drive immediately following the Cowboys taking a 3-0 lead. The Williams and Barham play led to Caleb Downs swarming off the edge to get in on a short-yardage fourth down stop of Derrick Henry, which was easily the moment of the season up to that point for Christian Parker’s defense. Dallas took this short-field possession right down the field again and this time got Williams into the end zone for six, jumping ahead 10-0. Dallas rallying back from down 24-13 to lead 28-24 also came off a short-yardage stop. The Ravens answered a scoring drive capped off by Ferguson’s touchdown and Lamb’s two-point conversion with a quick strike drive that saw three explosive plays of at least 20 yards, but got denied in short-yardage again. On 4th-and-goal from the one, Kenny Clark won as the low man at the point of attack, and Barham shot through the gap like a cannon to make the tackle on Henry. The Cowboys even flipped the script on making big plays for skill players looking easy to cap this go-ahead drive, as KaVontae Turpin found plenty of room to run after the Ravens motioned late to a two-high shell look on his jet sweep attempt. The Cowboys offense has gotten better out of condensed formations after being too spread out and ineffective in week one at the Giants, but still lack the physical identity which other teams that major in these formations have. This doesn’t necessarily have to be a bad thing if the Cowboys still play to the skills of their players, but with Ferguson off a two touchdown game versus the Commanders, his opportunities to stretch the field against the Ravens were shrunk. Brian Schottenheimer did not have the best feel for this game as play-caller. The best things the Cowboys will be able to take from this game in spite of all this offensively was their push in the run game, as well as the way they forced the Ravens to play two-high safety looks, and took advantage of them. The Ravens played with clear respect for the dynamic ability of both Lamb and Pickens, which was on display enough for the Cowboys to win this game, yet there was still a steady dose of throws behind the line of scrimmage that didn’t work, screens, and other ineffective plays that become more memorable in a bad loss instead. Flipping the good/bad coin yet again to this point though, the Cowboys were denied any opportunity to run the ball after first down in their final possession after Luke Schoonmaker’s false start penalty. The passing game did have some more room to work on 2nd-and-goal from the seven, and drew another one of these shell looks, but nobody got open and Prescott scrambled for a short gain. Then came the third down chance that was never really a chance for George Pickens, with Prescott and Schottenheimer revealing after the game the ball was apparently supposed to be thrown away there given the Ravens look, although Pickens was open. The defense made enough splash plays in this game to expect an offense with this much talent to capitalize on the situations it was handed. It’s still hard to fathom the Cowboys offense didn’t pass the test – losing to a Jesse Minter defense for the second year in a row. The final play before the game-winning FG put the worst possible cap on this being a coaching loss for the Cowboys, as they were willing to go through the growing pains of a new defensive scheme at the start of this season under Parker. With that said, the bread and butter for Parker’s scheme is supposed to be an umbrella style zone. New Sunday Night Football analyst Mike Tomlin even said at halftime of Rams at Broncos that he would expect any defense to be in an umbrella in that situation. Instead, the Cowboys inexplicably played man-to-man, didn’t get a pass rush, and saw Flowers get inside of Reddy Steward for the decisive blow. Mike Tomlin dives deep into the Ravens walk-off FG AND shouts out the Commanders OC for fantastic game management. 📺 Sunday Night Football: Rams at Broncos on NBC & Peacock pic.twitter.com/v9hrf5p42W — Sunday Night Football on NBC (@SNFonNBC) September 28, 2026 This was also one final field position win for the Ravens. The Cowboys did not trust Brandon Aubrey to keep the ball in the field of play on a “dirty kick” after having two kickoffs go out of bounds earlier in the game. Aubrey kicked a touchback instead, starting Baltimore at their 35-yard line, while no time also came off the clock on the kickoff. It is hard to remember any other recent Cowboys loss where all three phases of offense, defense, and special teams had clear-as-day moments that greatly contributed to losing the game. To make matters more muddy, we’ve covered…

summary: Sunday’s loss was costly for the Dallas Cowboys. In addition to being the losing team, the Cowboys lost a handful of players to injuries. Whether or not the field in Brazil was the primary culprit was a matter up for serious debate both before and during the game on the CBS broadcast, but whatever the […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Sunday’s loss was costly for the Dallas Cowboys. In addition to being the losing team, the Cowboys lost a handful of players to injuries. Whether or not the field in Brazil was the primary culprit was a matter up for serious debate both before and during the game on the CBS broadcast, but whatever the case, the Cowboys have players who are banged up. That would, obviously, make him a candidate for injured reserve. Cowboys S Jalen Thompson (hamstring) is set to miss “four-plus weeks” after being injured on Sunday in Brazil, EVP Stephen Jones said. IR stint most likely coming for Thompson. — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) September 28, 2026 The Cowboys already have one safety on injured reserve in P.J. Locke. Malik Hooker has also been hurt, and it remains to be seen when he will be able to return. Things hardly get easier for the Cowboys in the immediate future. They have a road game this week in Houston, so not terribly far, and then a short week next week as they host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night.
