title: Broncos Stock Up, Stock Down: Week 3 Comeback Win vs. Rams
summary: What a thriller! The Broncos move to 2-1 after an improbable, thrilling second-half comeback win. It was a tale of two halves for the Broncos, who trailed the Rams 16-0 at halftime before scoring 30 points in the second half. They had three offensive touchdowns, two successful two-point conversions, a pick-six, and a game-winning interception […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos celebrates a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the fourth quarter at Empower Field At Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images What a thriller! The Broncos move to 2-1 after an improbable, thrilling second-half comeback win. It was a tale of two halves for the Broncos, who trailed the Rams 16-0 at halftime before scoring 30 points in the second half. They had three offensive touchdowns, two successful two-point conversions, a pick-six, and a game-winning interception in the end zone. It was a crazy game that kept Broncos fans on the edge of their seat until the very end. It is also a complicated one for stock up and stock down because this game had multiple layers of good and bad throughout. So, we have plenty of players with their stock going up and others, unfortunately, with their stock going down. Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos roster and give you stock-ups and stock-downs on every player currently on the 53-man roster. After a bounce-back performance like that on Sunday, we are going to see a lot more stock-ups than we did last week. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock up: It was a complicated night for the Broncos quarterback. He was on the struggle bus in the first half and nearly had two ugly interceptions. The offense looked lifeless, and Nix simply was not playing well. However, this was a classic Bo Nix/Denver Broncos comeback victory. That means Nix came alive in the second half and had three touchdowns, including the eventual game-winner. His only blemish was an interception after a defender hit his arm. This allowed the Rams to take a 4th quarter lead, which is exactly what Nix wanted. He would go on to get yet another 4th-quarter comeback win. It wasn’t all great, and the stat book will not wow you, but the Broncos came back and beat a team many believe to be a Super Bowl contender. Nix had a great second half, and while it would be great if he could put together a complete game for once, I will take whatever leads to a Denver Broncos victory. Jarret Stidham – Unchanged : Is the veteran backup QB Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: Remains the emergency third-string quarterback Running Back JK Dobbins – Stock down: We simply need more from Dobbins, who does not look like the back who was top 3 in rushing last season before his injury. He averaged a poor 2.9 yards per carry and never really got anything going in the run game. He did have a few nice first-down carries, but overall, we need more from Dobbins. RJ Harvey – Stock up: Harvey didn’t do much in the run game, but he did have 6 receptions for 41 yards and led the team in receptions. It wasn’t anything to write home about, but he is filling his role and contributing as a pass catcher. Jonah Coleman – Stock down: I am including him here even though he is on the IR. Injuries suck, and he was on the verge of carving out a real role in this backfield. Unfortunately, he suffered a high ankle sprain vs. the Jaguars and played through it. This showed his toughness, and that game showcased his talent, but it was a poorly timed injury that killed the momentum he built in Week 2. Tyler Badie – Stock up: Like Harvey, he is playing his role and doing it well. He served as the third-down pass blocker and even went one-on-one vs. Aaron Donald and held his own. Badie also had 1 reception for 12 yards. Again, nothing crazy, but he’s playing his role and doing well at it. Adam Prentice – Stock down: Why did they even keep a fullback? 3rd-and-1 shotgun plays, and Prentice only played 4 offensive snaps. Could have used him a few times last night. Wide Receiver Jaylen Waddle – Stock down: Waddle’s stock was high last week, but it came crashing back down in Week 3. He had 2 catches for 10 yards and struggled to get anything going against this talented Rams secondary. You expect more from Waddle in these big games, but he simply didn’t produce. He did have a nice two-point conversion catch, which was big, but outside of that, it was a pretty forgettable night for the Broncos playmaker. Courtland Sutton – Unchanged: Sutton had a mostly quiet night, but did see 7 targets, which led to 3 receptions for 46 yards. Again, nothing to write home about, but a decent showing by the Broncos veteran pass catcher. Pat Bryant – Stock up: Bryant was the star of the night on the offensive side of the ball. He only caught two passes, but he turned those two passes into 2 catches for 44 yards and 1 touchdown. He also added a two-point conversion in there as well. His touchdown got the team on the board in the second half and his two pointer would tie the game at 16-16. He would later have a 39-yard catch-and-run on a 2nd and 20 late in the 4th quarter to set up the Broncos eventual game-winning touchdown. Bryant also drew the controversial DPI call late to give the Broncos an automatic 1st down and extend their late 4th quarter drive. Troy Franklin – Unchanged: Franklin played just 12 snaps and saw 1 target but like last week, he made the most of that 1 target. After Bryant’s 39-yard catch-and-run, Franklin followed that up with a 21-yard reception to get the Broncos offense rolling. His role is certainly diminished, but with Mims sidelined, he is making the most of his limited opportunities. Marvin Mims – Stock down: He has been hampered by injuries and not having a great start to his contract year. Hopefully, he can get healthy, and the Broncos can get their All-Pro returner and big-play specialist back. Lil ’ Jordan Humphrey – Stock down: Was inactive and doesn’t seem to be playing as much with Davis Webb running the offense. Kolbe Katsis – Stock up: The undrafted rookie had an adventurous night that included a couple of bobbled punt returns, a big return that sparked the offense, and attempting to hurdle multiple Rams players only to get hammered. Still, he made his NFL debut and has appeared in more games than most of the Broncos’ 2026 rookie class. Tight End Adam Trautman – Unchanged: He played in 40% of the Broncos’ offensive snaps but did trail Evan Engram in snaps, which is interesting. Evan Engram – Stock up: The production isn’t there, but the usage is. Engram had 2 targets and 0 catches on the night, but did play 60% of the snaps, which led all tight ends. He is getting the playing time, but the production hasn’t matched yet. Nate Adkins – Stock up: Is Nate Adkins the true Joker? Adkins caught his second touchdown of the season and now has back-to-back games with a touchdown. He played 34% of the snaps but seems to have a trusted role in the passing game when out there. Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: The rookie tight end continued to be inactive. Offensive Line Garett Bolles – Unchanged: The veteran LT has had a great start to the season, and while he did see a penalty called on him late in the game, he played well overall. I am, again, not an offensive line expert. Ben Powers – Unchanged: Looks like he struggled with the interior pass rush a few times, which is a strength of this Rams defense, but I did not notice him being good or bad either way. Luke Wattenberg – Unchanged: Like Powers, he struggled with the interior rush at times, but I did not notice him being good or bad throughout the game. Quinn Meinerz – Stock up: He sent Aaron Donald back to retirement. Mike McGlinchey – Unchanged: Had some issues with the speed rush, which is normal with McGlinchey, but from my untrained eye, he played solid. Alex Palczewski – Stock up: He played just 6 snaps, but that’s an increase. I would like to see the Broncos utilize their heavy packages more and pound the ball. Matt Peart – Unchanged: He didn’t play Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: He did not play Kage Casey – Unchanged: Inactive Defensive Line Zach Allen – Stock up: The Broncos’ pass rush ran hot and cold throughout the night, but when it was on, it was due to Allen being a disruptor. He had…

title: NFL Week 4 power rankings: Confidence in Jared Goff has Detroit Lions on the rise
summary: In Week 3, the Detroit Lions (2-1) took on a New York Jets team that was sporting one of the best defenses in the NFL to start the 2026 season. After landing near the top of most defensive statistical categories, the Jets looked like a much bigger challenge than the Lions had faced. Yet, when […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) waves at fans after 31-24 win over New York Jets at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In Week 3, the Detroit Lions (2-1) took on a New York Jets team that was sporting one of the best defenses in the NFL to start the 2026 season. After landing near the top of most defensive statistical categories, the Jets looked like a much bigger challenge than the Lions had faced. Yet, when the lights came on at Ford Field in Detroit, quarterback Jared Goff was once again stellar, leading the Lions to 400 total yards of offense (more than the Jets allowed in their previous games combined) and scoring 31 points for the third game in a row. While the Lions’ defense is still a major question mark and needs improvement, most national analysts believe Goff and his supporting cast—most notably Jahmyr Gibbs—are playing at such a high level that the Lions can outscore most other teams. As a result, the Lions are moving up, or staying neutral, in this week’s national power rankings. Let’s take a closer look. The Athletic: 6 (Previous rank: 8) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : QB confidence: Should be higher If former Lions defensive coordinator Aaron Glen thought he was going to rattle Jared Goff, he was sorely mistaken. The New York Jets blitzed Goff 16 times Sunday, and the 31-year-old was 16-for-16 for 173 yards and two touchdowns on those plays. For the season, he has five touchdowns, no interceptions and a completion percentage of 86.7 when blitzed, according to TruMedia. Overall, he leads the league in touchdown passes (eight) and hasn’t thrown a pick. USA Today: 10 (Previous rank: 10) From Nate Davis : How consistent has this offense been? Exactly 31 points in every game. A low of 355 yards and a high of 381. And just one turnover. If a defense that’s allowed the most points (95) in the league can hold on long enough to get some reinforcements, this team has a legit shot at finally ending the league’s longest hex of failing to qualify for the Super Bowl. Sporting News: 11 (Previous rank: 14) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions need every bit of what Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs are doing to light it up offensively with their defense porous in every which way. Shootouts follow everywhere they go and they might need to make a drastic change soon. CBS Sports: 12 (Previous rank: 15) From Pete Prisco : Jahmyr Gibbs is carrying this team and is in the early MVP conversation. They have to be happy to be 2-1 with all the defensive injuries. Yahoo Sports: 13 (Previous rank: 13) From Frank Schwab : The Lions have given up the most points and second-most yards in the NFL this season. They beat the Jets on Sunday but allowed 335 yards and 24 points. Two Jets, Garrett WIlson and Kenyon Sadiq, had 100-yard receiving games. Most Lions games this season will be high scoring. They’ll need the defense to make a few plays, like it did in the final minute. The Jets reached the Lions’ 28-yard line, but safety Chuck Clark sacked Geno Smith on a blitz, causing a fumble that the Lions recovered. “And then for our defense to have to, man, they had to make that stop,” Lions head coach Campbell said. “That’s what it was going to come down to. And it was such a great call by [defensive coordinator] Kelvin Sheppard and those guys executing it.” ESPN: 13 (Previous rank: 14) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Fantasy surprise: QB Jared Goff It’s sometimes easy to forget about Goff’s consistency because he plays alongside elite playmakers such as RB Jahmyr Gibbs and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown. The veteran QB is a viable starter in fantasy this season, averaging 21.9 points. Goff was the 18th-best quarterback in our draft rankings and had an ADP of 131.4. After Sunday’s win, Gibbs lauded Goff as Detroit’s “leader.” “We trust him with everything,” Gibbs said. NFL.com: 14 (Previous rank: 13) From Nick Shook : We know the Lions can put up points in bunches by leaning heavily on Jahmyr Gibbs, and this offense is capable of keeping them in every game they play. Their defensive struggles in the fourth quarter remain concerning, even if a takeaway saved them from another trip to overtime. Sports Illustrated: 14 ( Previous rank: 18) From Connor Orr : Jared Goff is one of six quarterbacks in NFL history to start the season with more than 800 yards passing and eight touchdowns in three games. If the Lions can go out and get themselves Joey Porter, all will be right in the world, as the offense is holding up its end of the bargain.

title: Lions vs. Jets Song of the Game: ‘Dashboard’ by Modest Mouse
summary: After a brief hiatus, “Song of the Game” has returned, back by popular demand of our Editor in Chief and Sticktator, Jeremy Reisman. While I’ve been absolutely swamped between work, writing/editing, podcasting, being a husband and a parent, the next half hour I’ll spend writing this is a welcome break of such serious bellyaching about […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets congratulates Head Coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions with their 31-24 win after the game at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a brief hiatus, “Song of the Game” has returned, back by popular demand of our Editor in Chief and Sticktator, Jeremy Reisman. While I’ve been absolutely swamped between work, writing/editing, podcasting, being a husband and a parent, the next half hour I’ll spend writing this is a welcome break of such serious bellyaching about the secondary. Lions vs. Jets Week 3 Song of the Game: “Dashboard” by Modest Mouse Growing up in the day and age of burning CDs to create the soundtrack of your bus rides to and from school, Modest Mouse was a staple of my collection. “Float On” and “Ocean Breathes Salty” spun a bunch on my Sony D-EJ360 Walkman . It hit me right in the midst of my percolating angst as middle school tested my place in the world, and Modest Mouse was just what the doctor ordered . “Dashboard” is the lead single from the band’s fifth studio album—a track guitarist and songwriter Johnny Marr, formerly of The Smiths, worked on during his first day riffing with Modest Mouse. It’s much more dance-driven pop rock than the slacker rock the band debuted with a decade prior, but even in a different flavor, it’s still damn good. Modest Mouse’s lineup has changed a bunch over the band’s life cycle, as has the Detroit Lions coaching staff over Dan Campbell’s six years as head coach. Aaron Glenn was one of my favorite hires Campbell made at the start of his tenure, and what he managed to accomplish as a defensive coordinator in 2024 was nothing short of remarkable. It led him to taking a head coaching position with the New York Jets the year after, and while it was a rocky start for the former Jets cornerback, he’s undoubtedly got that team in a position that feels eerily similar to the way Campbell had the Lions in 2022. They’re still feeling out the way to win, but they’re right there—and with tons of draft capital in this upcoming draft. Oh, it should’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know Well, you told me about nowhere well it sounds like someplace I’d like to go Detroit’s defense is still very much a work in progress, especially on the backend, and that’s not something you want to hear about a football team through three weeks of regular season play. Many drew tired of Glenn’s unwillingness to spy mobile quarterbacks, and found him to be overaggressive by the end of his time in Detroit, and we’re seeing how any place other than where we’re at with this defense is someplace we’d like to see it go. Well, it would’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know Oh, the dashboard melted, but we still have the radio And yet, with as bad as the defense has been—with the dashboard melted—we still have the Lions offense playing their same ol’ tunes. 31 points in three straight games, and this game would’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know had it not been for this offense keeping this team in the win column. Well we scheme and we scheme but we always blow it We spent all week waiting to see the adjustments Kelvin Sheppard and the defense would make after getting embarrassed on “Thursday Night Football.” What sort of adjustments could they possibly make to clean up that mess? But up until the fourth quarter, the Lions held the Jets to just 10 points. Detroit had a comfortable 24-10 lead, they had schemed and schemed… but they ended up blowing that lead, letting the Jets tie the game with a little over four minutes remaining in the game. We’ve yet to crash, but we still might as well tow it Standing at a light switch to each east and west horizon Every dawn you’re surprising And in the evening one’s consoling Saying, “See it wasn’t quite as bad as.” Four plays later, the Lions have the lead, the defense forces a game-winning turnover, and I spent my op-ed this week reminding everyone that while the Lions’ dashboard is melted, we’ve yet to crash, and the radio’s still working, so we might as well enjoy it. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here .

title: Detroit Lions facing crossroads with Cade Mays, Juice Scruggs
summary: Through three weeks of the season, Detroit Lions backup center Juice Scruggs has been one of the better NFL players at the pivot. Scruggs’ PFF grade of 71.5 current ranks fourth among all NFL centers, and Scruggs ability to be a force in the run game (78.7 run defense grade, second-best) has helped Detroit regain […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 27: Quarterback Jared Goff #16 and center Juice Scruggs #70 of the Detroit Lions during the second half of an NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 27, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Through three weeks of the season, Detroit Lions backup center Juice Scruggs has been one of the better NFL players at the pivot. Scruggs’ PFF grade of 71.5 current ranks fourth among all NFL centers, and Scruggs ability to be a force in the run game (78.7 run defense grade, second-best) has helped Detroit regain some of the rushing efficiency that was lost last season. The Lions currently rank sixth in rushing success rate (48.2%) per NFL Pro and fourth in average yards before contact per carry (2.06). During his weekly radio appearance on 97.1 The Ticket, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell had high praise for how Scruggs has played so far. “He really fits us,” Campbell said. “He’s a pro. Man, he’s high energy. He’s the same guy every day. He busts his tail, and he’s getting better. He’s getting better for us at the center position. So, man, he’s a good fit for us.” This offseason, the Lions acquired Scruggs in a trade that sent David Montgomery to the Houston Texans. At that point, Scruggs was in line to be a top reserve at both the center and guard positions. But after Cade Mays suffered a broken wrist early in training camp, Scruggs was pulled out of the competition for starting left guard and plugged in as the starting center. However, the Lions are nearing an interesting crossroads with Scruggs. Lions coach Dan Campbell gave an update on Mays’ recovery from the wrist injury, and it sounds like he could return to the team somewhere around their Week 6 bye. “Right now, we’re kinda hoping around the bye, somewhere in there,” Campbell told 97.1 The Ticket on Tuesday morning. “Before or after the bye with him, but he’s doing a great job. He really is.” That begs the question: what do you do with Scruggs when Mays is healthy and ready to go? The Lions gave Mays a three-year, $25 million contract to be their center for the next few years, so it seems unlikely Detroit would keep him sidelined. But if Scruggs is still playing well, it would be hard to bench him, too. Campbell was asked by radio host Jon Jansen if Scruggs would re-enter the competition at left guard to potentially start there, and the Lions’ coach offered a brief and powerful answer. “Absolutely.” Campbell was not asked if he would consider keeping Scruggs as the starting center. Right now, the starting left guard position is being held by Christian Mahogany, but he was in tight competition with Ben Bartch before a foot injury sidelined Bartch recently. Campbell praised how Mahogany played against the Jets. “I thought he had a winning performance,” Campbell said. “I thought he played good enough for us to win. I thought he ran off the football. I thought he was violent, played a physical game. There’s a couple of these little things he had got his feet out of whack that he’s got to clean up, just staying honed in on the technique of it. But, that’s it, man. Just the consistency.” The majority of Scruggs’ experience in his three previous seasons in the NFL has been at the guard position, but in 2024, he started eight games at center and produced 64.5 PFF grade, good for 19th out of 38 qualifying centers over that span. He also started 13 games at center in his final year at Penn State in 2022. Mays is not eligible to come off of injured reserve until after this week’s game against the Carolina Panthers. After that, we’ll have to see how Detroit opts to shake out the rest of their offensive line.

title: Joey Porter Jr. trade: Weighing the pros, cons of Detroit Lions making the move
summary: Rumors have been swirling for weeks, but the Joey Porter Jr. trade speculation peaked on Sunday when several national reporters said the Detroit Lions were among a “handful of teams” who have reached out to the Pittsburgh Steelers inquiring about the availability of the 26-year-old cornerback. Per the same reports, the Steelers are open to […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 12: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers breaks up a pass during the fourth quarter in the NFL 2025 game against the Cleveland Browns at Acrisure Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rumors have been swirling for weeks, but the Joey Porter Jr. trade speculation peaked on Sunday when several national reporters said the Detroit Lions were among a “handful of teams” who have reached out to the Pittsburgh Steelers inquiring about the availability of the 26-year-old cornerback . Per the same reports, the Steelers are open to listening to offers but “would want a strong compensation package”—which is vague and obvious. At the tail end of this week’s Lions vs. Jets recap PODcast, our crew discussed the pros and cons of the Lions making such a move. Sunday’s game reminded us again that Detroit’s outside cornerbacks are currently a liability. Even their CB1, D.J. Reed, has struggled through the first few weeks of the season. Beyond that, the Lions are still tinkering with their best option at second outside cornerback. Is it Rock Ya-Sin, who was strong last year but was effectively benched in Week 3? Is it Roger McCreary, who has flashed at both outside and nickel, but also struggled against the Jets? Or is it Ennis Rakestraw, who looked very solid in a small situational role on Sunday and doesn’t have a ton of experience? If there are that many questions at cornerback, doesn’t Porter provide some answers? But adding talent isn’t just a matter of whether the player will help the team or not. Porter would undeniably improve Detroit’s defense. The cost, however, is something that the Lions will have to deeply grapple with. It’s unclear right now how much Porter would cost, but on the PODcast, we go through some recent cornerback trades to gauge the market. And that’s only half of the conversation about trading for Porter. The Steelers cornerback is also seeking a contract extension as he currently rides out the final year of his rookie deal. Would Porter be willing to play out the final year without an extension in Detroit? That’s unclear, but the Lions will have to seriously consider inking him to a long-term deal if they acquire him, and the team has been doing a delicate salary cap balancing act for the last couple of years now that they have some top-end market deals on the books. If Detroit trades and signs for Porter, how much will that disrupt their current plans for 2026 and beyond? Will it cost them their ability to re-sign some of their players, or can they cook the books enough to make this happen without jeopardizing their future? There are two more facets of this potential trade to consider: First, how good is Porter? Fans tend to get stuck on one or two players and romanticize them without considering their weaknesses. Will Porter be able to come in and immediately play like a CB1? Another thing to consider is whether Lions general manager Brad Holmes would even do it. While he’s made in-season trades before, he has never added a young, long-term piece and extended them before they’ve even played a down in Detroit. This would mark a pretty big break from Holmes’ reputation, but is it finally time for him to adjust his strategy? We discuss the entire topic below on this week’s PODcast. title: Discussion: Rank the NFC North after 3 weeks of the 2026 season
summary: We’re three weeks in the 2026 NFL season, and we’re starting to figure out a lot about teams. Though sample sizes are still pretty small, and it’s hard to fully judge a team when we don’t really know too much about the opponents they’ve played. So any sort of sweeping judgments should be avoided. But… […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings and head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears meet on the field following the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re three weeks in the 2026 NFL season, and we’re starting to figure out a lot about teams. Though sample sizes are still pretty small, and it’s hard to fully judge a team when we don’t really know too much about the opponents they’ve played. So any sort of sweeping judgments should be avoided. But… the NFL news cycle is 24/7, and there’s nothing wrong with a little analysis after one-sixth of the season is through. Yes, teams will continue to get better or worse. Yes, injuries will continue to alter the trajectory of each team. But why not have a little fun before we get too deep into the season? The NFC North standings are probably a little surprising to most, although it certainly isn’t a shock to see that three of the four teams are sporting a winning record. As a reminder, here’s how things look after Week 3: Minnesota Vikings: 3-0 Detroit Lions: 2-1 Chicago Bears: 2-1 Green Bay Packers: 1-2 So today’s Question of the Day is: How would you rank the NFC North after three weeks of the season? My answer: Let’s start with something I think almost everyone can agree on right now: the Packers look definitively like the worst team in the division. They are a somewhat miraculous comeback away from starting the season 0-3, and their drubbing at the hands of the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday was embarrassing on all levels. Their offense (23rd in points scored) is broken, with an offensive line that is being held together by scotch tape. Their defense (29th) may somehow be worse. They aren’t only the worst team in the division right now, they have a solid argument for a bottom five team in football. That could change if they get some things figured out on offense, but it looks bad right now. Note: they are 30th in DVOA. The other three teams are difficult to rank. The Vikings have the best record because of their insane defense (first in DVOA, second in points allowed). However, their offense remains pretty stagnant (30th in DVOA, 17th in points scored). The Bears are coming off a very impressive win over the Eagles on Monday night, but we can’t forget how much the Vikings humbled them at home in Week 2—holding them to just three points. The Lions have one of the most efficient offenses in football (third in scoring, eighth in DVOA), but their defense is a massive liability right now (32nd in scoring, 28th in DVOA). The only thing that is clear to me is that you have to put the Vikings ahead of the Bears because of the head-to-head win. That leaves the Bears and the Lions, and I think both teams are in similar boats. Their offenses are going to be awesome and reliable this year, but they’ve got serious questions about their defense. Honestly, though, I trust the Bears’ defense a little more, because of their consistent ability to force turnovers. So my ranking right now would be: Vikings Bears Lions Packers How would you rank the four NFC North teams after three weeks? Share your thoughts in the comment section below by joining our community. title: 2 Detroit Lions defenders who earned more playing time, per Dan Campbell
summary: The Detroit Lions made a handful of personnel changes for their Week 3 game against the New York Jets, and a pair of them earned more playing time moving forward after putting up strong performances. Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the media on Monday morning following his re-watch of the team’s 31-24 victory over […]
full_text: Detroit Lions linebacker Trevor Nowaske (53) tackles New York Jets wide receiver Sterling Shepard (87) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions made a handful of personnel changes for their Week 3 game against the New York Jets, and a pair of them earned more playing time moving forward after putting up strong performances. Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the media on Monday morning following his re-watch of the team’s 31-24 victory over the Jets, and he noted that both linebacker Trevor Nowaske and cornerback Ennis Rakestraw played well enough in their expanded roles on Sunday to earn more time on the field. Nowaske played in half of the defensive snaps—more than any linebacker not named Jack Campbell or Derrick Barnes, usurping the role from Devin White—and Dan Campbell was very clear why. “Nowaske just does everything right. He just does,” Campbell said. “He’s been doing that now for a while, came in, had a really good camp, and he’s a very disciplined player. He’s grown a ton since he’s been here, and just turned himself into a real solid player. He just does things right, man. You know that whole thing that we talk about: be where you’re supposed to be when you’re supposed to be there? That’s him. He’s exactly where he’s supposed to be when he’s supposed to be there. He makes plays.” Nowaske’s discipline was fully on display against the Jets. Campbell pointed to a play in the red zone, where Geno Smith pitched it out to the fast and elusive Breece Hall, and Nowaske was ready for the perimeter run play. He chased Hall down for no gain. “We gave him that rep in practice the other day—coaches did a great job—he yawned at it,” Campbell said. “And then when we get in the game, same thing. He doesn’t miss a beat.” With the amount of missed assignments and failed run fits against the Bills, Nowaske brought assignment-sound play that helped the Lions hold the Jets to just 58 rushing yards and 3.1 yards per carry after Buffalo rushed for over 200 yards. “He’s going to continue to get opportunities because he’s earned that,” Campbell continued. “He’s a valuable special teams player for us, and there’s a role on defense where he can help us.” As for Rakestraw, the Lions’ 2024 second-round pick was in the game situationally against the Jets. When the Lions moved to nickel sets, they kicked Roger McCreary inside and brought Rakestraw in to play the outside. Per PFF, Rakestraw allowed just a single catch on four targets, and he had an impressive pass breakup against Jets No. 1 receiver Garrett Wilson. “Rakestraw, I thought, showed up,” Campbell said, unprompted. “He’s going to get more ops here. I thought he showed up. That was promising.” When asked about how they may expand Rakestraw’s role, he said the plan is still to keep him on the outside, but he wouldn’t rule out eventually giving him reps at the nickel, too. Ultimately, he just believes that because Rakestraw still hasn’t had a ton of playing time, there’s still a chance he can bloom into a valuable, regular contributor. He was even encouraged by some of the growth Rakestraw showed through training camp, prior to an ankle injury that sidelined him late. “I think Rake’s got a chance, man,” Campbell said. “He’s got the ability, and he wants to do it right. He works at it, and I do. I think the more opportunities he gets, the better he’ll get.” This week, both players will have their hands full with a Carolina Panthers offense that has been explosive at times this year. They are currently fifth in points scored, averaging 29.7 points per game and lead the league in passing yards per game (295.7).

title: Detroit Lions stock report: 19 risers, 7 fallers against the Jets
summary: Much like their Week 1 win against the New Orleans Saints, the Lions started the second half strong before allowing the fourth quarter to become far too close for comfort. Similarly, the defense was largely responsible for allowing explosive passing plays that fueled the Jets’ comeback efforts, but it delivered a clutch play when it […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets is sacked by D.J. Wonnum #98 of the Detroit Lions during the first quarter at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Much like their Week 1 win against the New Orleans Saints, the Lions started the second half strong before allowing the fourth quarter to become far too close for comfort. Similarly, the defense was largely responsible for allowing explosive passing plays that fueled the Jets’ comeback efforts, but it delivered a clutch play when it mattered most to seal the victory. Sunday’s win against Aaron Glenn’s Jets wasn’t pretty, but there were signs of improvement. The offense started slowly but continued to acclimate under Drew Petzing, while the defense stopped the run effectively, got home against Geno Smith in several high-leverage moments, and played well in the first half, allowing just one touchdown drive across the Jets’ first five possessions. Of course, Geno Smith catching fire and torching the pass coverage with improbable completions into tight coverage felt almost inevitable, and there’s still plenty to clean up defensively. Nevertheless, this was another stepping stone toward becoming a better team, rebuilding the Lions’ identity, and preparing for their next opponent, the Carolina Panthers, on Sunday night. Survive and advance. The Lions got the win, and now they have another opportunity to build on it. Let’s get into the Week 3 stock report following Detroit’s second win of the season. Stock up: Jahmyr Gibbs, RB Jahmyr Gibbs again showed why he is magically delicious to root for and rely on. Like a leprechaun finding a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, Gibbs heel-clicked his way into the end zone on his third trip there Sunday for the game-winning score. No matter how hard the Jets tried to focus on catching Gibbs—they’re always after me Lucky Charms—they couldn’t contain him. Since Gibbs entered the league in 2023, there have been only 23 individual games in which a player recorded at least 150 yards from scrimmage and three touchdowns. After torching the Jets for 164 total yards and three touchdowns on 27 touches, Gibbs is now the only player to accomplish the feat four times over that span. Jonathan Taylor is the only other player to even do it three times. Not bad against a defense that was allowing less than 200 total yards per game prior to Week 3. Gibbs is the engine of the Detroit Lions offense, contributing to 11 of the team’s 24 first downs on the day. And while he somehow uncorked a Barry Sanders-esque, full-field cutback run, remarkably, that 17-yard scamper was his longest play of the afternoon. He didn’t kill the Jets with long gashes. Instead, it was an incredibly mature, patient performance as a runner. Gibbs consistently paced his runs, waited for his offensive line to drive defenders, found creases, and churned out positive yardage. Pair that with his efficiency in the receiving game, and Gibbs continually kept the Lions offense moving without needing the explosive plays that usually define his highlight reel. Stock up: Alim McNeill, DT Between his contract extension, season-ending injury, recovery, underwhelming season back from injury, and ironman workload, Twinkle Toes has spent plenty of time in the spotlight among Lions fans and some media, usually with some degree of scrutiny. Against the Jets, the Lions’ enigmatic defensive tackle received a more manageable workload and was arguably their best defender on the field. McNeill was a wrecking ball who heated up as a pass rusher in the second half, consistently finding an edge, particularly against center Josh Myers and right guard Joe Tippmann. He even lined up at times like a hooper lurking menacingly in a two-point stance before attacking the pocket. McNeill had only one game with more than three quarterback pressures last season, per NFL Pro, and his seven pressures against the Jets tied for the most he’s recorded in a game since Week 11 of 2022. His timely red-zone sack was massive, but his impact extended well beyond it. Two other pressures directly led to sacks for the defense, another forced an incompletion, and his physical work in the run game helped limit carries to minimal gains finished off by second-level defenders. It was an encouraging performance against a good interior offensive line, and one McNeill can build on. Stock down: D.J. Reed, Roger McCreary, & Rock Ya-Sin, CBs The veteran cornerback trio were the main culprits in the Jets’ comeback effort. Oftentimes, they were in tight, physical coverage and simply lost out on contested catches or precision throws placed where only the receiver could reach them. Still, their performances won’t cut it against better passing offenses, and they nearly cost the Lions on Sunday. Reed, McCreary, and Ya-Sin combined to allow 12 catches on 15 targets for 166 receiving yards (13.8 yards per reception), two touchdowns, zero pass breakups, and three penalties. Reed and McCreary each allowed a perfect 158.3 passer rating when targeted. Ya-Sin practically walked onto the field and was immediately handed a defensive pass interference penalty, much to the dismay of the Lions fanbase. Too much biting and grabbing from the entire lot of them. Reed will bounce back with stronger games in coverage, as he showed against the Bills, and McCreary deserves a little more runway in his part-time outside cornerback role in base defense alongside his nickelback duties. But Garrett Wilson, the Jets’ tight ends, and even Isaiah Williams got the best of this bunch on Sunday. Stock up: Penei Sewell & Blake Miller, OTs What a relief it was to get Blake Miller back, even if you hardly knew he was there—in a good way. The further along this season gets, the more Miller gets to settle in at right tackle, while Penei Sewell continues to look increasingly like a lockdown natural protecting Goff’s blind side. Sewell was a force in the run game, pushing interior defenders downfield like a blocking sled on runs up the middle, sealing off the edge on runs off his tail, and being a menace on the backside to ensure there was no leakage and Gibbs had cutback lanes when needed. Miller wasn’t quite as dominant in the run game, but he grabbed his lunch pail and went to work while also being nearly spotless in pass protection against second-overall pick David Bailey and Will McDonald IV. The afternoon wasn’t completely spotless, with Sewell flagged for a hold that wiped out a productive Gibbs run and Miller committing a false start, but those were rare blemishes on an otherwise strong performance from Detroit’s bookends. Gibbs’ 5.0 yards before contact per rush was the eighth-best mark of his career, and it wasn’t inflated by any untouched, full-field explosive runs. His 65.0% success rate was also the fourth-best of his career, with the offensive line—and these two hog mollies in particular—playing a major role in that success. With only the fourth-and-one failed attempt being the one costly negative run play. Miller hitting and the Lions potentially having cornerstone bookends for at least the next five seasons would go a long way toward this offense remaining a juggernaut and extending Detroit’s championship-caliber window. Stock up: 2024 Draft Class – Ennis Rakestraw Jr. CB, Sione Vaki, RB, Christian Mahogany, LG Kidnappers aside, the over-discussed, dead-horse-beaten, much-maligned draft class from the draft in Detroit had three players active Sunday who, still only at the beginning of their third seasons, continue to carve out roles and all contributed to helping the Lions secure a victory. While McCreary started at outside cornerback, Rakestraw came in and took over that role in obvious passing situations, playing 23 snaps—a third of his career snaps—with 22 coming on passing plays. He rose to the occasion, often matched up with Wilson, who caught only one of four targets against Rakestraw…
author: Al Karsten

title: The secondary is bad, but the Detroit Lions are not
summary: The Detroit Lions are 2-1, adding to their win column after knocking off an up-and-coming New York Jets team. But if you check the temperature of the more reactionary corners of the fanbase, they’re unimpressed and uninspired. After the shortcomings on defense snowballed—yet again—in the fourth quarter of Sunday’s game, those unimpressed feel little confidence […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the New York Jets with Jameson Williams #1 during the third quarter at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are 2-1, adding to their win column after knocking off an up-and-coming New York Jets team. But if you check the temperature of the more reactionary corners of the fanbase, they’re unimpressed and uninspired. After the shortcomings on defense snowballed—yet again—in the fourth quarter of Sunday’s game, those unimpressed feel little confidence in this team’s chances when it comes to accomplishing big-picture goals. But really though, why care so much in the here and now about Super Bowl viability? Why are people talking about this team like the playoffs start in a couple weeks? It’s not even October! The team with a winning record has some warts in the secondary, but after spending a weekend out and about, chatting with folks from the grocery store to the golf course and dive bars in between, you would have thought they were a winless bunch of sucks; a hopeless group watching their window slam shut on their fingers. The secondary is bad. That doesn’t mean the Lions are bad. And coming to a verdict on their ceiling based on their performances through three weeks is premature. That’s not me being dismissive of the very serious problems in the secondary. Be it some mix of coaching, scheme, and/or personnel, Geno Smith shouldn’t have done what he did in Week 3. Smith’s +21.1 completion percentage over expected, defined by NFL Next Gen Stats as, “the difference between a quarterback’s actual completion percentage and expected completion percentage controlling for the level of difficulty of each pass,” was nearly 11% higher than the quarterback who finished second in Week 3 (Patrick Mahomes, +10.25). Smith was second in tight-window rate (27%), the percentage of passes where the targeted receiver has less than 1 yard of separation when the pass arrives. It appears as though Nevin Lawson crawled so Roger McCreary could also come up just shy of making a play . The secondary was in better position to make plays this week, but there were still missed assignments, miscommunication, and missed opportunities to make a play and get off the field on third down. The guys on the backend still have to make plays in coverage, not just on blitzes where they’re forcing game-winning turnovers—nothing like waiting until the very last moment, Chuck Clark! It’s with much regret that it’s my job to inform you the secondary for the Detroit Lions is in rough shape. Despite you knowing that their starting safeties are both on PUP, and their No. 1 cornerback as of three months ago is now facing up to life in prison as a member of the Seattle Seahawks, here’s a chance to remind you the most turbulent spot on the roster is experiencing some choppy air while they’re attempting to build the plane with the wheels up. The issues in the secondary are all anyone can talk about, so we’re going to see people ignore the rest of the defense’s performance against the Jets. “I just can’t ignore the secondary’s play and pretend like this is a team capable of contending for a Super Bowl” is the low-hanging, drive-time topic of conversation after this most recent game. They’ll ignore Geno Smith getting sacked five times for 44 yards. Pretty sweet the pass rush is second in time to pressure (2.46 seconds) and 10th in quarterback pressure rate (39.0%)! And what about that run defense, eh? 3.1 yards per carry, third in stuff rate (percentage of run plays resulting in no gain or loss: 26.3%), and sixth in rushing EPA per play allowed (-0.23). Some things to hang your hat on if you’re Kelvin Sheppard, but it doesn’t mean it’s time to rest. It never is in the NFL, and there’s still plenty of work to be done. Also, more good news: there’s no reason to assume the secondary you see now will be the one this team has in January! It sure doesn’t sound like Brad Holmes and the front office are waiting until it’s too late to try and improve at the cornerback position after early-morning reports Sunday about the Lions showing interest in Joey Porter Jr. If it doesn’t end up being the big name in Porter Jr., maybe that player Detroit needs could come from any other number of the 0-3 teams with their playoff hopes actually on life support. Imagine watching that game against the Jets, getting to see Jahmyr Gibbs pass Billy Sims for second place in rushing touchdowns by a Detroit Lion in eight fewer games, and still letting the secondary ruin your afternoon. The offense scored 30+ points for the third consecutive game without a Ben Johnson in sight and you’re letting the cornerbacks get you bent out of shape? Are you new here? Were you around when the practice field hill was built and the ping pong tables removed? At the end of the day, the Lions won despite their significant weakness in the secondary rearing its ugly head at the worst possible moment, but there is plenty of time for roster tinkering that could address their glaring weaknesses. Detroit is 2-1, and you haven’t even nailed down a date for a trip to the pumpkin patch. Take a look around the NFC: if there’s a world beater, point ‘em out. There isn’t a single team around here that is free from defects. There’s a long way between now and Week 18, so until then, buckle up if you’re in for the ride.

title: Panthers could be down 2 key defensive backs vs. Lions
summary: The Detroit Lions are entering Week 4 as three-point favorites over the Carolina Panthers in their Sunday night showdown, but some injury news from Monday could see that line shift (note: it’s already jumped to 3.5). According to NFL reporter Tom Pelissero, the Panthers’ No. 1 cornerback Jaycee Horn is out indefinitely after suffering a […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jaycee Horn #8 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates during an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are entering Week 4 as three-point favorites over the Carolina Panthers in their Sunday night showdown, but some injury news from Monday could see that line shift (note: it’s already jumped to 3.5). According to NFL reporter Tom Pelissero, the Panthers’ No. 1 cornerback Jaycee Horn is out indefinitely after suffering a quad injury on Sunday against the Browns. Horn is coming off back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons with the Panthers, and he signed a four-year, $100 million extension last offseason. He was off to another decent start to the season, allowing just five catches on 10 targets for 63 yard and two pass breakups, according to PFF. To make matters worse for the Panthers, in Sunday’s loss to the Browns, they also lost their other starting outside cornerback Mike Jackson to a groin injury. There has yet to be an update on his status, but he suffered the injury in the first half and did not return to the game. Jackson is an eight-year vet who actually spent some brief time with the Lions in 2019, but has really turned things around lately. In 2025, Jackson produced an NFL-high 19 passes defended and also logged four interception. Left in the Panthers’ cornerback room is fourth-round rookie Will Lee III, Akayleb Evans, and nickel corner Chau Smith-Wade. Carolina also has three practice squad cornerbacks: undrafted rookie DeVonta Smith, and two undrafted players from the 2025 class: Zion Childress and Corey Thornton. Of the three, only Thornton has any real experience at the NFL level, playing in 12 games and 127 defensive snaps last season. This will be something to monitor as the week goes on, but I would expect the Panthers to add to that room as they prepare for a dynamic Detroit Lions passing attack that currently ranks eighth in passing yards (247.7 per game), third in passer rating (116.1), and tied for second in passing touchdowns (eight).

title: Detroit Lions Week 3 snap counts: Breaking down defensive changes vs. Jets
summary: After starting the season 1-1 with glaring holes in defensive execution, the Detroit Lions made some significant changes to their personnel, some of which helped them get back on track, leading to a 31-24 win over the New York Jets in Week 3. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 27: Detroit Lions linebacker Trevor Nowaske (53) and his teammates celebrate a big yardage kickoff return by Detroit Lions running back Jacob Saylors (not pictured) during the second quarter of a regular season NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions on September 27, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After starting the season 1-1 with glaring holes in defensive execution, the Detroit Lions made some significant changes to their personnel, some of which helped them get back on track, leading to a 31-24 win over the New York Jets in Week 3. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 65 (100%) Josh Dobbs: Did Not Play After a bumpy start to the game, Goff settled in quickly and continued his high level of play. While you’d like to see the offense sharp from start to finish, it’s hard to argue with the offense putting up 31 points in all three games so far this season. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 45 (69%) Sione Vaki: 20 (31%) — 15 special teams snaps (65%) Jacob Saylors: 2 (3%) — 15 (65%) Gibbs was once again a human highlight reel in this game, but Aaron Glenn’s Jets exposed a possible weakness: pass protection. Glenn’s repeated A-gap blitzes were a problem for Gibbs, and likely why Vaki saw his snaps increase, as he was terrific in pass protection. Vaki’s ability to contribute in the run and pass game proved to teams that he’s not just a one-trick player that will tip the offensive play call. Vaki talked with Pride of Detroit after the game and discussed his growth since the beginning of the season: “The preparation going into these past two weeks, going out there and letting loose, and not being afraid to mess up. Being able to believe in myself, supported by (running backs) coach (Tashard) Choice and the boys in the room, has helped push me forward and has been a real confidence builder.” Vaki went on to discuss how he tries to be the aggressor in pass protection: “It’s definitely a conscious choice. Watching the film of (Jets) Demario Davis, being the great linebacker that he is, we knew he was going to try and run through our faces, and I just knew I had to respond by stuffing my face in there. There’s still some things to clean up, but today’s game did feel good.” And for those worried that threatening the blitz could be a way for defenses to get Gibbs off the field, the Lions did respond by running some 21 personnel, with both Gibbs and Vaki on the field at the same time. A nice counterpunch by offensive coordinator Drew Petzing. Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 53 (82%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 48 (74%) Isaac TeSlaa: 31 (48%) Tay Martin: 2 (3%) — 15 (65%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 8 (35%) With the Lions deploying some heavier sets against the Jets—13 personnel and Jumbo packages saw upticks in usage—the Lions wide receivers saw their opportunities scaled back a tick. Snap distribution remains very similar to past weeks, but it wouldn’t be surprising if this is St. Brown’s lowest snap count this season. Tight end Sam LaPorta: 60 (92%) Brock Wright: 38 (58%) — 10 (43%) Jackson Meeks: 10 (15%) — 2 (9%) Tyler Conklin: DNP ( INACTIVE ) As mentioned above, the Lions deployed a fair amount of 13 personnel in this game, with the wrinkle being that they split Meeks out wide to stretch the Jets’ Base defense. There will be games moving forward that the Lions will want a more balanced TE3 like Conklin on the field, but this new wrinkle with Meeks illustrates the versatility this group has. Offensive line LT Penei Sewell: 65 (100%) LG Christian Mahogany: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%) C Juice Scruggs: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%) RG Tate Ratledge: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%) RT Blake Miller: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%) T Larry Borom: 15 (23%) — 5 (22%) G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (22%) C Seth McLaughlin: DNP LG Ben Bartch: DNP ( INJURED ) With their preferred starting five healthy again, the offensive line played very well in this game, slowing down a Jets defense near the top of all defensive rankings entering Week 3. Overall, the Lions gave up just eight pressures and two sacks, but the offensive line accounted for only five pressures and was not to blame for either sack. As previously mentioned, the Lions leaned on their Jumbo sets in this game, utilizing Borom as a sixth offensive lineman for nearly a quarter of offensive snaps. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 48 (73%) — 3 (13%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 33 (50%) — 2 (9%) — 1 offensive snap (2%) DT Tyleik Williams: 30 (45%) — 3 (13%) DL Levi Onwuzurike: 11 (17%) 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP ( INACTIVE ) The defense made a lot of personnel adjustments in this game, with the first clear change being the scaling back of McNeill’s snaps. While 73% is still a big percentage, that’s about the spot he’s been at in the past when he’s been his most productive. His seven pressures and a sack illustrate this was a smart decision. With McNeill scaling back a bit, that opened up the opportunities for his backup, rookie Skyler Gill-Howard, to increase his workload, and he rewarded them with three pressures and a half-sack (he split with Aidan Hutchinson). Gill-Howard spoke with Pride of Detroit following the game and discussed his first NFL sack: “The guard (Jordan Meridith), he was the second one because the first (Dylan Parham) got hurt—I knew I could beat him laterally, so that’s what I did; I took an inside counter, and while I got a little past the quarterback, the D-line did a good job of forcing him up, allowing me to spin out and get it—and of course, Hutch was right there.” Gill-Howard also saw one snap on offense on a goal-line run that resulted in a Gibbs touchdown. Although the play went in the opposite direction of Gill-Howard’s block, it looks like a precursor to something the Lions could build on moving forward. “You know coach (Dan) Campbell. You’ve seen those types of plays throughout his tenure here. He told me during training camp that he was going to put something in and we came up with ‘that’ for now, and we’ll see what happens in the future.” EDGE EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 64 (97%) — 1 (4%) Rush End DJ Wonnum: 44 (67%) — 3 (13%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 19 (29%) — 5 (22%) Rush End Derrick Moore: 9 (14%) Rush End Eric O’Neill: 1 (2%) — 13 (57%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP ( INACTIVE ) While McNeill saw his reps scaled back a bit, the Lions ramped Hutchinson’s up, as he only took two defensive snaps off all game. Despite facing what looked like constant double teams, Hutchinson still managed five pressure and the half-sack mentioned above. Typically, when the Lions deploy three-linebacker sets, they lean on a Big End (Tyler Lacy) to work opposite Hutchinson, but that wasn’t the case on Sunday. Wonnum saw his snaps increase in multiple formations beyond what we have seen from a rush end in the past. Wonnum also rewarded the team for the move, delivering three pressures and two sacks. Linebacker MIKE Jack Campbell: 66 (100%) — 3 (13%) SAM Derrick Barnes: 57 (86%) — 1 (4%) SAM Trevor Nowaske: 33 (50%) — 17 (74%) WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 19 (29%) — 7 (30%) WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga: 0 (0%) — 17 (74%) MIKE Jimmy Rolder: 0 (0%) — 15 (65%) WILL Devin White: DNP ( INACTIVE ) Campbell continues to play every defensive rep, and Barnes only misses a handful of snaps a game, but the LB3/4 spot saw a big shakeup in this game. White, previously in a starting role, was a healthy scratch, giving Rodriguez the start at WILL. However, the big change came with Nowaske, who was deployed all over the field and was on the field for half the game. Pride of Detroit spoke with Nowaske after the game and asked him if his increased usage was opponent-specific, or something that was a result of his performances in practice and games. “It could be a combination of both. I know I am a good linebacker in this league.…

title: Green Bay Packers News: Brian Gutekunst makes an attempt to fix offensive line
summary: Offensive line? Yeah, consider that fixed. The Packers have signed not one (Cordell Volson), not two (Laken Tomlinson), but three (Mekhi Becton) linemen that nobody else wanted to put on their 53-man roster. Checkmate, everybody else. Contender status has been restored in Green Bay. Color me underwhelmed by the Packers’ sudden urgent desire to fix […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 11: Mekhi Becton #73 of the Los Angeles Chargers looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL wild card playoff game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on January 11, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Offensive line? Yeah, consider that fixed. The Packers have signed not one (Cordell Volson), not two (Laken Tomlinson), but three (Mekhi Becton) linemen that nobody else wanted to put on their 53-man roster. Checkmate, everybody else. Contender status has been restored in Green Bay. Color me underwhelmed by the Packers’ sudden urgent desire to fix their offensive line. Though Brian Gutekunst has seemingly answered fans’ pleas to add to the offensive line, we should have healthy skepticism about any lineman available in late September. The last few seasons of NFL football have shown the world the value of a good offensive line (and the Packers have shown what can happen with a bad one, for that matter), and I don’t think anybody’s just letting good prospects sit at home on their couch when they play a position as important as we understand the line to be. Still, at least they’re doing something, right? The Packers’ trio of offensive line acquisitions are all former starters. Not all of their previous work is good, mind you, and Tomlinson in particular is well into the “journeyman” phase of his career, though he was once a Pro Bowl caliber player. They may be limited now, but each of them has a more impressive resume than anyone the Packers have put on the field at guard to this point. Even if Tomlinson’s Pro Bowl came when Donovan Jennings still had two seasons of college ball to go, he’s a far sight more accomplished than his younger counterpart. It boils down to this: at least they’re doing something. Is it too little too late? Quite possibly, even probably. But at least it’s something, and if it makes the Packers more watchable for the rest of the season, they’ll have accomplished something. Packers working on offensive line from different angles | Packers.com I like this approach much better than the “don’t work on the offensive line at all” idea they went with for the first three weeks. Can Mekhi Becton and other veterans signings save Packers offensive line? | Packers Wire Even if the answer here is “probably not,” trying something is better than not trying anything. Matt LaFleur believes Packers offense needs to deliver more ‘body blows’ | Packers News ($) If the Packers can figure out a way to grind out a few yards on the ground, it could open things up for the rest of the offense. Packers-Buccaneers Matchups: Both Teams Have Huge Advantages | Sports Illustrated I don’t want to hear about any advantages the Buccaneers have. How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list | ESPN This article makes a big deal about how Myles Garrett has averaged 14 sacks a year for the last five seasons, but it doesn’t really focus much on how he’d have to keep up that pace for more than five more seasons to break the all-time sack record, and he’d be 37 by the time he does it. California duo set Lego World Map record in under 5 hours | UPI I like a good Lego as much as the next guy, but this is pretty intense. title: Packers Roster Update: Green Bay reshuffles roster for OL additions
summary: This week, the Green Bay Packers added Laken Tomlinson, formerly on the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad, to their 53-man roster, and Mekhi Becton Sr., previously on the street, to their practice squad. With a full roster, both on the 53 and practice squad, the Packers needed to make two corresponding roster moves to make room […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, the Green Bay Packers added Laken Tomlinson, formerly on the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad, to their 53-man roster, and Mekhi Becton Sr., previously on the street, to their practice squad. With a full roster, both on the 53 and practice squad, the Packers needed to make two corresponding roster moves to make room for the Tomlinson and Becton additions. On Monday, the team announced that they have placed right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, who had a complete tear of his Patellar tendon, on the injured reserve. It’s unlikely that Bako-Bewele will play another game for the Packers in 2026, and they have a big decision to make about his future next offseason. ZBB, who was not designated to return from the IR, makes space for the addition of Tomlinson. To add Becton as Green Bay’s fifth practice squad offensive lineman, the Packers released defensive tackle Eric Johnson II, who was the only interior lineman on Green Bay’s practice squad. The Packers are a bit “oversigned” at the defensive tackle position on the 53-man roster, as they have seven players on the active roster, but with 15 offensive linemen in practice now, they’re clearly “oversigned” at the offensive line position, too. For what it’s worth, there’s some crossover between Tomlinson, Becton and the Packers’ offensive scheme. Tomlinson was in San Francisco when Green Bay offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich was the 49ers’ assistant offensive line coach from 2017 to 2018. Tomlinson also played under offensive coordinators Mike LaFleur, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur’s brother, and Nathaniel Hackett, Green Bay’s offensive coordinator from 2019 to 2021, in the 2022 and 2023 seasons for the New York Jets. Becton was also a Jet for two years under Mike LaFleur (2021 and 2022). — Here’s a recap of the Packers’ full roster moving forward: Quarterback (3) 53: Jordan Love and Tyrod Taylor PS: Kedon Slovis Running Back (5-6) 53: Chris Brooks, Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd Exempt: Josh Jacobs PS: Pierre Strong Jr. and Damon Bankston Receiver (7-9) 53: Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, Jayden Reed*, Skyy Moore, Bo Melton and J.
