title: Patriots vs. Jaguars snap counts from Week 3
summary: While quarterback Drake Maye unsurprisingly drew most of the attention after the New England Patriots’ loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars — he turned the ball over three times and now stands at seven on the season — his performance was far from the team’s only issue. The offensive line, for example, also had its fair […]
full_text: While quarterback Drake Maye unsurprisingly drew most of the attention after the New England Patriots’ loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars — he turned the ball over three times and now stands at seven on the season — his performance was far from the team’s only issue. The offensive line, for example, also had its fair share of issues yet again, especially on the right side. Not only was backup right tackle Greg Van Roten lost to a thigh injury in the second quarter, right tackle Morgan Moses also looked hampered by the foot injury he was already dealing with leading up to the game. This plus the game’s blowout nature contributed to a change being made in the late third quarter: Moses was pulled from the contest, with first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu entering in his place. It was the first time in his young career the rookie saw extended snaps on the offensive side of the ball after playing four snaps in Week 2 against Pittsburgh. In total, he was on the field for 26 snaps versus the Jaguars, 20 as a right tackle in place of Moses and six more as an extra blocking tight end. However, that does not mean Lomu is now pushing for the starting job. “Not that I’m aware of,” said head coach Mike Vrabel after the game. “I didn’t have a chance to watch the tape, but it was like, ‘Let’s get Caleb some reps.’ We were down however much we were down, a s—tload. That was just me making a decision. … It’s a long season. Morgan is 36 years old. Didn’t think we were going to come back and win the game. As much as I wished that we were, I didn’t think that we were. So, I made a decision.” Here is our full snap count report from the Patriots’ 35-6 loss at Jacksonville’s EverBank Stadium . Offense Total snaps: 63 | Time on the field: 27:05 | *denotes starter LT Will Campbell* (63; 100%), LG Alijah Vera-Tucker* (63; 100%), QB Drake Maye* (51; 81%), C Jared Wilson* (51; 81%), WR Mack Hollins* (48; 76%), WR Romeo Doubs (46; 73%), TE Hunter Henry* (44; 70%), RT Morgan Moses* (43; 68%), RG Walter Rouse (41; 65%), WR DeMario Douglas (37; 59%), RB Rhamondre Stevenson* (33; 52%), RT/TE Caleb Lomu (26; 41%), RB TreVeyon Henderson (23; 37%), WR Kyle Williams (22; 35%), RG Greg Van Roten* (22; 35%), WR Efton Chism III* (16; 25%), TE Tanner Arkin (15; 24%), QB Tommy DeVito (12; 19%), C Ben Brown (12; 19%), TE Cameron Latu (9; 14%), RB Corey Kiner (8; 13%), FB Reggie Gilliam* (8; 13%) With the game already getting out of hand in the late third quarter, the Patriots decided to mix things up down the stretch. This meant removing quarterback Drake Maye and center Jared Wilson from the contest; the two were replaced by backups Tommy DeVito and Ben Brown. Brown entered the game as the backup behind Wilson and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker, with late-August trade acquisition Walter Rouse the backup right guard behind Greg Van Roten. When the latter went down, Rouse entered the contest over the more experienced Brown — a decision that was explained by Mike Vrabel on Monday. Elsewhere on offense, the Patriots relied on their usual cast of characters. Two players still stand out: Tanner Arkin, who was a healthy scratch last week out-snapped a struggling Cameron Latu as the second tight end; Reggie Gilliam, who started the game and was thought to be an integral part of the offense this season, played only eight snaps all day. Defense Total snaps: 62 | Time on the field: 31:06 | *denotes starter LB Robert Spillane* (59; 95%), S Kevin Byard III* (59; 95%), LB Christian Elliss* (57; 92%), CB Carlton Davis III* (54; 87%), CB Christian Gonzalez* (52; 84%), S Jaylen Reed* (52; 84%), ED Elijah Ponder* (51; 82%), ED Gabe Jacas* (49; 79%), DT Milton Williams* (41; 66%), CB Marcus Jones (36; 58%), DT Cory Durden* (32; 52%), DT Christian Barmore (28; 45%), DT Joshua Farmer (24; 39%), DT DaQuan Jones (23; 37%), DT Jeremiah Pharms Jr. (13; 21%), CB Charles Woods (12; 19%), S Mike Brown (12; 19%), ED Jose Ramirez (8; 13%), LB Darius Muasau* (8; 13%), LB Namdi Obiazor (3; 5%), LB Erick Hunter (3; 5%), CB Channing Canada (3; 5%), CB Karon Prunty (3; 5%) The Patriots had no 100% defenders on Sunday, another byproduct of the late-game rotation caused by the game script. Among the starters pulled early was Christian Gonzalez, who was seen having a conversation on the sideline with head coach Mike Vrabel before his day ended. As for the playing time numbers Jaylen Reed is a player to highlight. Filling in for the injured Craig Woodson, he started and effectively went wire-to-wire with the other starters. The third safety role, which was occupied by Dell Pettus before he placed on injured reserve last week, was filled by practice squad elevatee Mike Brown. That said, Marcus Jones also occasionally rotated into that position. On the edge, where the Patriots were down Dre’Mont Jones (inactive) and Quintayvious Hutchins (injured reserve), youngsters Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas received a heavy workload. The two had some moments but like the rest of the defense were unable to make the game-saving plays. The Patriots also gave their depth pieces some reps on Sunday. Backup cornerbacks Charles Woods, Channing Canada and Karon Prunty all entered the game late, as did linebackers Namdi Obiazor and Erick Hunter. Darius Muasau was in the same boat, but interestingly enough started the contest as an off-ball linebacker alongside Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss in the team’s 4-3 base grouping. Special teams Total snaps: 23 | Time on the field: 1:49 LB Namdi Obiazor (20; 87%), S Mike Brown (19; 83%), TE Cameron Latu (17; 74%), CB Karon Prunty (15; 65%), LB Darius Muasau (14; 61%), CB Charles Woods (14; 61%), LB Erick Hunter (13; 57%), S Jaylen Reed (12; 52%), FB Reggie Gilliam (11; 48%), TE Tanner Arkin (9; 39%), DT Cory Durden (9; 39%), ED Gabe Jacas (8; 35%), WR Mack Hollins (7; 30%), ED Elijah Ponder (7; 30%), ED Jose Ramirez (7; 30%), RB/KR Corey Kiner (6; 26%), WR/KR Kyle Williams (6; 26%), LB Robert Spillane (6; 26%), DT Milton Williams (6; 26%), DT DaQuan Jones (6; 26%), K Andy Borregales (6; 26%), P/H Mitch Wishnowsky (5; 22%), LS Julian Ashby (5; 22%), WR/PR Efton Chism III (4; 17%), OT Will Campbell (3; 13%), OT Caleb Lomu (3; 13%), OL Alijah Vera-Tucker (3; 13%), OL Walter Rouse (3; 13%), OL Ben Brown (3; 13%), CB/PR Marcus Jones (3; 13%), CB Channing Canada (3; 13%) The Patriots went through three personal protectors last week against the Steelers, and they made another change versus the Jaguars. With neither Dell Pettus nor Craig Woodson playing in the game, and with Jaylen Reed elevated to a starting role at safety, Mike Brown served as PP for Mitch Wishnowsky’s two punts on Sunday. The role is not a new one for Brown, who has played it throughout his four years in the NFL and also in training camp. As for switching things up, the typical return group of KR Kyle Williams and PR Marcus Jones was complemented by Corey Kiner and Efton Chism on Sunday. Kiner ran back one second-quarter kickoff 31 yards, even though it was brought back by a penalty. Chism had an 18-yard punt return on the second-to-last play of the game. Did not play N/A Considering the game’s blowout nature, the Patriots decided to use their entire game day squad against the Jaguars. Inactive QB3 Behren Morton, TE Eli Raridon, OT Dametrious Crownover, DT Leonard Taylor III, ED Dre’Mont Jones, S Craig Woodson The Patriots were down two defensive starters against the Jaguars, with Dre’Mont Jones and Craig Woodson both unavailable due to shoulder injuries sustained last week versus Pittsburgh. In addition, a thigh injury suffered in Week 2 kept No. 2 tight end Eli Raridon out of the contest as well.

title: Patriots vs. Jaguars: The good, the bad, the s—t that gets you beat
summary: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. Welcome back, 2024 […]
full_text: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. Welcome back, 2024 New England Patriots! While this is an exaggeration, of course, Sunday’s 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars brought back some painful memories of what was ultimately a lost season for the organization. The Patriots were thoroughly outclassed in all three phases of the game, suffering their worst loss of the Mike Vrabel era and dropping to 1-2 on the year. With that all being said, let’s dive into our weekly breakdown of the good and the not-so-good from the blowout loss in Jacksonville. The good: Opportunities for backups Yes, we are grasping at straws here. Obviously, the Patriots had some positive moments even in a 29-point loss. Drake Maye hit a few chunk plays; Will Campbell provided quality play at left tackle; Marcus Jones hauled in an interception; Christian Gonzalez continued to be his shutdown self; Rhamondre Stevenson didn’t fumble. And: the team’s backups like second-string quarterback Tommy DeVito got some rare opportunities to take the field in a regular season setting. All in all, however, the good was not just out-weighed by the bad — it didn’t even register on the scale. That’s how bad this loss was, and why we are choosing an admittedly arbitrary positive to take away from it. The bad: Penalties Whether or not Sunday’s game was truly representative of New England’s capabilities this season remains to be seen; the Patriots suffering bad early-season losses in Florida are not exactly a new invention in 2026. That said, it is clear that the team’s margin for error particularly in light of some personnel losses over the first three weeks is marginal especially against quality teams. This is why getting flagged nine times is not a winning way to play football for the Patriots. Those penalties cost the team 68 yards, but they were more impactful than that. For example, a Morgan Moses hold negated a 21-yard Drake Maye touchdown run. On the very next play, Romeo Doubs was flagged for offensive pass interference, pushing the team back an additional 10 yards and turning 1st-and-10 at the Jacksonville 21 into 1st-and-30 at the 41. There were back-to-back neutral zone infractions (by Gabe Jacas and Elijah Ponder), a taunting penalty that turned 4th-and-1 into 4th-and-16 (by Mack Hollins), and a block above the waist to undo a 31-yard kickoff return (by Cameron Latu). Long story short: penalties were an issue in all three phases, and they came in all varieties. Not necessarily a glowing endorsement for the team’s discipline, and the coaching staff’s ability to enforce it. The s—t that gets you beat: Virtually everything else Usually, there isn’t one singular area that led to a team scoring only six points on offense while simultaneously giving up 35. The Patriots’ loss in Jacksonville was no exception. There were Drake Maye’s continued ball security issues, as in: one Football Follies -worthy lost fumble and a pair of dubious decisions resulting in interception. There was some bad blocking up front, especially on the right side of the line where the team was down to a third-string guard and playing a hobbled right tackle. There was a wide receiver group failing to get consistent separation. That’s just the offense. On defense, the Patriots allowed the Jaguars to go 5-for-5 in the red zone and 8-for-12 on third down (including a 17-yard touchdown in the third quarter). The unit did register one interception, but other than that was unable to affect the quarterback or his supporting cast. On special teams, Andy Borregales shanked a 38-yard field goal try, the aforementioned penalty erased what would have been a long kickoff return, and Kyle Williams fielded what could have been a kick out of bounds for an effective net loss of 31 yards. It just was not good enough there, or anywhere else. “We blocked a guy in the back to start [a] drive, backed up. We don’t use the rules to our advantage on the sideline with the kick,” Mike Vrabel said from the Gillette Stadium podium on Monday. “We turn the ball over, and then we don’t take the chances on defense when we have chances to turn the ball over, turn it over. They executed in the red zone; we clearly didn’t. We missed a field goal. The game got away from us after that. But it could have been a lot of ‘what ifs.’ It could have been 14-9 easily, to where you are in a competitive football game, you can get a turnover, but instead of that, it’s 21-3.” As noted above, the Patriots’ margin of error is slim at the moment. Any one of the issues the team had on Sunday could have made life difficult. The combination of all of them turned the game into the blowout it was.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Mike Brown, Jeremiah Pharms Jr. revert to Patriots’ practice squad following Week 3
summary: Veterans Mike Brown and Jeremiah Pharms Jr. reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Monday after serving as standard elevations at EverBank Stadium. The 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars marked the first game action of the 2026 regular season for the safety as well as the defensive tackle. Brown, 26, recorded one […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots defensive tackle Jeremiah Pharms Jr. (98) in the first half against the Philadelphia Eagles at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Edward Finan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Veterans Mike Brown and Jeremiah Pharms Jr. reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Monday after serving as standard elevations at EverBank Stadium. The 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars marked the first game action of the 2026 regular season for the safety as well as the defensive tackle. Brown, 26, recorded one stop against running back Bhayshul Tuten while handling 12 snaps on defense and 19 snaps on special teams. With Dell Pettus on injured reserve and Craig Woodson on the wrong side of questionable due to a shoulder injury, he worked as the third safety on Sunday afternoon behind captain Kevin Byard III and trade acquisition Jaylen Reed. Entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2022, Brown spent time on the practice squads of the Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings and Cleveland Browns before heading to the Tennessee Titans’ 53-man roster late in his rookie campaign. The Miami of Ohio product remained in Nashville until he was not tendered as a restricted free agent last March. He signed in Foxborough soon after and joined the practice squad after being released as a vested vet at the cutdown deadline. Brown now stands 36 appearances, including a handful of starts, into his career. The 6-foot-1, 218-pound safety has had a hand in 61 tackles and two passes defensed across 515 snaps on defense and 779 snaps in the kicking game. Pharms, 29, got the start on Sunday for a base front that was missing veteran outside linebacker Dre’Mont Jones due to a shoulder injury and also recently lost rookie edge Quintayvious Hutchins to injured reserve . The 6-foot-2, 300-pound defensive lineman notched one tackle in run support and stayed in for 13 defensive snaps. New England brought Pharms back on the initial practice squad after he cleared waivers as part of the August cutdown. He now finds himself 32 games, including six starts, into his series of transactions with the organization. Undrafted out of Sacramento City College, San Joaquin Delta College and Friends University in 2020, the ex-linebacker made stops with the Champions Indoor Football League’s Wichita Force and USFL’s Pittsburgh Maulers before entering the NFL ranks prior to training camp in 2022. Pharms’ Patriots tenure has brought 46 tackles, two sacks and one fumble recovery across 607 snaps on defense and 128 snaps on special teams. Two standard elevations remain for both call-ups before 53-man agreements would be required to take the field. For now, head coach Mike Vrabel’s 1-2 team moves forward with an open spot on the active roster. The Buffalo Bills host next Sunday’s AFC East opener at Highmark Stadium. Kickoff is set for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Mike Vrabel explains Patriots’ offensive line usage after Greg Van Roten injury
summary: The New England Patriots’ offensive line has taken a handful of hits early this season. On Sunday, that came in the second quarter when veteran right guard Greg Van Roten, who drew the start for Mike Onwenu (injured reserve), left the game early with a thigh injury.  He was replaced by Walter Rouse, not Ben […]
full_text: The New England Patriots’ offensive line has taken a handful of hits early this season. On Sunday, that came in the second quarter when veteran right guard Greg Van Roten, who drew the start for Mike Onwenu (injured reserve), left the game early with a thigh injury. He was replaced by Walter Rouse, not Ben Brown, who was the team’s top interior backup last season. “Walt has been working there. We felt confident that was the plan going in, that Ben Brown would be the center and then the first left guard in. That’s where he had been working,” head coach Mike Vrabel explained. Rouse allowed a team-high four pressures and a sack in relief, potentially opening the door for Brown to take over at right guard moving forward. “It’s good to have Ben back healthy. I’m sure he will help us; he’ll probably have to help us this week,” Vrabel said. “I thought Walter had a few mistakes, but he competed and will have to improve. I’m sure Ben will be a part of that process going forward, and we will see where Greg Van Roten is here after a few more tests.” Brown started four games for the Patriots last season at left guard and signed a two-year, $6.6 million extension in December. He injured his knee this preseason and missed the regular-season opener. Rouse, meanwhile, switched from tackle to guard this summer with the Minnesota Vikings. The Patriots acquired him via trade for a late-round draft-pick swap during roster cuts.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots vs. Jaguars: Fan observations from Week 3 loss
summary: Well that sucked. After a Week 2 that saw them get their first win and look fairly stifling on defense against a Steelers team that just hung 30 on the Cincinnati Bengals, the Patriots went down to Jacksonville and laid an absolute egg. Just a listless, lifeless, lame performance all around. It’s still early in […]
full_text: Well that sucked. After a Week 2 that saw them get their first win and look fairly stifling on defense against a Steelers team that just hung 30 on the Cincinnati Bengals, the Patriots went down to Jacksonville and laid an absolute egg . Just a listless, lifeless, lame performance all around. It’s still early in the season, I know. But yikes. Yesterday saw the entire Northeast blanketed with rain, wind, and overall nastiness as the Patriots enjoyed a balmy, sunny game down in Florida. There was once a time when I would have lamented the fact that New England wasn’t playing at home, because I would have been at the game in a cheap poncho while doing my absolute best to get as much liquid down my gullet as I was getting all over my body. But I have long since aged out of that nonsense, and had (what was supposed to be) a very nice afternoon on the couch in my jammies with the first fire of the season coupled with the first nut brown ale of autumn. A little slice of heaven. Something else that comes with getting older: the realization that summer is wildly overrated. Everywhere is crowded, everything is expensive, and there’s all this pressure to really live it up between Memorial Day and Labor Day, as if there aren’t any other opportunities to be happy the other nine months of the year. Well I say nuts to that. Give me cooler weather, crisp nights, the smell of leaves and woodsmoke in the air, delicious beers, open windows, and all the sports back on TV. Not to mention a significantly lower electricity bill for those of us who may or may not be married to a woman who may or may not insist on sleeping in full pajamas with a down quilt on no matter the outside temperature and thus may or may not blast the AC at borderline-unholy temperatures. And “borderline-unholy” is as good enough a phrase as any to describe some of the things that came out of my mouth while I was watching that game. It wouldn’t be overly hard to chalk this one up as just one of those games. Every team has games like this where nothing seems to go right. Bad penalties, lame turnovers, missed kicks, inaccurate throws, poor tackling, lackluster play-calling… it happens. Brady and Belichick had more than a handful of games like that. And it’s easy to point out that if a few plays had gone differently — a made FG, a Drake Maye TD run not called back from holding, a little less air under a pass — we could be singing a different tune this morning. But given what we’ve seen through three weeks thus far, with an offense that has two TDs on a long run and a DPI-induced goal-to-go, it’s tough to just shrug this one off as a bump in the road. And it isn’t entirely on Drake Maye, but a lot of it is. What really has me worried right now (not to the point of panic, but the panic police are in the neighborhood and asking questions) is that maybe that shoulder injury Maye suffered last season was hidden or mismanaged and never fully healed right, and now he’s the latest RG3 or Carson Wentz who just never quite came back to his old self. I don’t mind physical errors. Balls slip out of hands (heh). You can trip over your own feet on occasion, a behavior that is widely gaining notoriety as “The Pop Douglas.” That happens. But we’re now seeing at least one horrendous decision per game from the quarterback that directly take points off the board. On the Travis Hunter pick, at absolutely no point was Efton Chism even remotely open. He was completely blanketed. The play was busted. You run out of bounds, you take the points, then you get back to work. These panic throws are just ruining everything, and I’m not sure what to do about it. The 2025 Patriots seemed to open every single game by letting their opponent march right down the field and score a TD before they actually got going. The 2026 Patriots seem to have abandoned that strategy and have instead opted for a promising drive short-circuited by an atrocious turnover. What he really needs is a get right game. A slump buster, if you will. Which makes me really happy that the Patriots have to go to Buffalo next week, that should be just what the doctor ordered. What I dislike the most, I think, is that I’m starting to get strong 2023 vibes from this team. In 2023, if the Patriots were down by seven or more at any point, that was more or less the game. They didn’t have the ability to come back from a two-score deficit. I haven’t seen anything from the 2026 team that gives me faith that they can do the same. And there’s no way you can sit here and say that this is all because A.J. Brown is out. He isn’t some magic fix-all that’s going to get this offense off the schneid. Unless the coaching staff built their entire system around a talented but enigmatic WR in his first year with a new team. And if that’s the case, we have much bigger problems than a QB with a bad case of the yips. Carlton Davis almost picked off a quick screen early in the second quarter just before Jacksonville’s first TD of the day, and I found myself remembering the time that Kyle Dugger picked off the exact same play against the Raiders a few years back. I had completely forgotten about that guy and had to look up what became of him (he plays for the Bengals in case you didn’t know or, like me, forgot he existed). Talk about a ton of upward momentum suddenly and inexplicably stopped for a guy who was slated to be a cornerstone of the team but then just kind of vanished. I wish that the Jags had had a 1st-and-10 inside the 20 which led to a touchdown that got called back which then became 1st-and-30 at the 40 which then became some razzle-dazzle nonsense that was a lucky break more than anything to scratching just enough yards back for the field goal attempt. Because that’s an objectively funny series of events and I would have liked to laugh at it. What’s going on with Kyle Williams? Where is he? Why isn’t he more involved? And if Maye so deeply trusted Stefon Diggs and Kayshon Boutte, why are they both gone? As I mentioned earlier, I spent this game on the couch, in my pajamas, in front of a roaring fire. And I feel like I was significantly less comfortable than Trevor Lawrence was all day. This team needs some players back, and soon. The defense isn’t playing poorly, per se, although they did seem to have some real tackling issues yesterday and gave up almost 140 yards on the ground. But it has to wear on a unit when your counterpart isn’t pulling their weight. We saw a 70-yard field goal attempt to close out the first half of this game. Cam Little had the distance, he just pulled it a little wide to the right. It’s just a matter of time before someone hits one. That means that the NFL is extremely close to presenting fans with a scenario where a touchback and one first down puts a team into scoring position. The sounds I have found myself making every time Drake Maye releases the ball are foreign to me. When Andy Borregales straight-up shanked that 38-yard attempt at the beginning of the third quarter, that was it. If you turned the TV off at that point, I don’t blame you. You didn’t miss much after that. I don’t think that the Jags looked overly dominant yesterday. That isn’t a knock on them at all; they did what they needed to do to win. But this wasn’t a scenario where the Jags straight up dominated the Patriots. New England just never showed up, at any level. And that might be the most troubling part. The good news is — and real good news this time, not the “laugh so you don’t cry” kind of stuff — after Buffalo, the Patriots enter a relatively soft (on paper, at least) part of the schedule. And outside of the Bills and the Chiefs, the entire AFC seems to be a mess of mediocrity. So things are far from over. Patriots seasons of yore are replete with early slumps that turned positive. So let’s all keep the faith. For now. This is the NFL, so watch the Patriots go to Buffalo next week and win 30-6. But, man, do I find myself wishing that this game was taking place at literary…
author: Alec Shane

title: Patriots News: Not enough lipstick for this pig
summary: If ever there was a game to dig a grave and bury the football, this was it. The headlines below tell most of the sordid tale, beginning with Drake Maye – and the coaching staff by proxy. This loss was a complete 3-phase effort. Last week I wondered if the win vs. Pittsburgh would start […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 27: Quarterback Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots is sacked by Defensive Tackle DaVon Hamilton #52 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the second half of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images If ever there was a game to dig a grave and bury the football, this was it. The headlines below tell most of the sordid tale, beginning with Drake Maye – and the coaching staff by proxy. This loss was a complete 3-phase effort. Last week I wondered if the win vs. Pittsburgh would start a streak, and now I’m wondering the same thing, but in reverse. The Steelers were one of eight teams that won yesterday after losing last week. (If they watched any Patriots highlights from Week 3, they probably felt even worse about Week 2.) But the point is, the team bounced back competitively and they beat the 2-0 Bengals. The Pats face the juggernaut Bills next week. Buffalo was a loss waiting to happen Sunday but overcame five turnovers to beat the Chargers 24-16, with Josh Allen punching in two rushing TDs and James Cook running for 154 yards. Can the Pats bounce back like that? Right now, the Magic Eight Ball waffles between “Very doubtful” and “Reply hazy, try again.” That’s what the entire team will have to do… Try again. TEAM TALK Post Game Notes , Patriots-Jaguars: Marcus Jones snags his first pick of the season, Efton Chism has first pass completion of his career, Caleb Lomu sees first action at right tackle, Mitch Wishnowsky had a 73-yard punt, the second-longest in his career; More. Evan Lazar ’s Game Observations: 8 takeaways from the 35-6 loss in Jacksonville. “The Patriots need to get their young quarterback right, and fast, or the season will get away from them…“ Gamebook: Full Patriots at Jaguars stats . Post Game Quotes: Patriots – Jaguars not yet available. Post Game Pressers: Mike Vrabel – Drake Maye – Christian Gonzalez, Marcus Jones, Kevin Byard III, Christian Elliss, and Romeo Doubs . title: Drake Maye looks broken. That doesn’t mean he can’t be fixed.
summary: Their 2023 season was one of the most frustrating in recent New England Patriots memory. It was not just that they won only four games all year, but that they were seemingly out of answers throughout. No matter what button head coach Bill Belichick pushed, the team and its third-year quarterback, who had shown promise […]
full_text: Their 2023 season was one of the most frustrating in recent New England Patriots memory. It was not just that they won only four games all year, but that they were seemingly out of answers throughout. No matter what button head coach Bill Belichick pushed, the team and its third-year quarterback, who had shown promise earlier in his career, kept spiraling as the losses continued to pile up. The Patriots of 2026 are not at that point. Their season is only three weeks old and their own third-year QB has shown that he can play the position at a significantly higher level than his predecessor, Mac Jones, ever had. And yet, the frustration and helplessness are starting to feel similar. And just like it was back then, it all starts at quarterback. Back in 2025, Drake Maye looked like one of the best QBs in football. Heck, he was one of the best QBs in football. He completed 72% of his passes during the regular season for 4,394 yards, 31 touchdowns and just eight interceptions. His 0.313 EPA per play among qualifying passers was the highest in the league, and he only narrowly missed out on the league MVP award while leading a team that had gone 4-13 in back-to-back seasons to division title and 14-3 record. It was impressive, but it also was a mirage — at least to a degree. The playoffs, after all, were a different story for the Patriots and their quarterback in particular. Maye’s regular season swagger seemed gone, and the success followed suit: his EPA per play dropped to -0.148, as his completion percentage tanked and turnover rate increased. Of course, it wasn’t all his fault. The offensive line, starting two rookies on the left side, felt apart; the receivers were unable to generate consistent separation; and the unit ran into four of the best six defenses in the league en route to the Super Bowl. Three games into the 2026 season, however, Maye again seems all out of sorts. Yes, the offensive line continues to have some problems — it’s the right side now — and the offseason changes at wide receiver have not yet paid the proper dividends. However, the problems seem to run deeper than that. Maye himself looks broken, and Sunday’s 35-6 loss in Jacksonville made this dramatically clear. In a way, it was a greatest hits collection of bad football from the MVP runner-up. He had a bizarre fumble in the first quarter (and another later in the game that he recovered). He gave away points when he forced a pass and threw an interception at the Jaguars goal line. He had another pick when he couldn’t connect with wide receiver Kyle Williams on a backside curl. Ultimately, he had to watch backup Tommy DeVito finish the game in his place . It was a low point both this season and in what had been a quite promising career up until last year’s playoffs. Now, the Patriots and Maye are faced with an uncomfortable truth: if they don’t transform it from a low to a turning point, their season could be over before it even began. Last year and under different circumstances the Patriots managed to do so. And even though they are dealing with a more daunting challenge this time around, they can do so again. The first step is identifying what the hell is even going on. For head coach Mike Vrabel, it seems the issue is not so much a physical but a mental one. Appearing on WEEI on Monday, he used golf as an analogy. “We really want to make a good score. Sometimes, we’re so focused on it that we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways,” he said. “We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in, and go play football, and not try to force things that aren’t there.” Three games into his third season, forcing things has been one of Maye’s biggest problems. He forced passes in the season opener against the Seahawks, single-handedly costing his team the game and later admitting he simply ran out of patience. He made another questionable decision in Week 2 versus Pittsburgh, and then again on the aforementioned goal-line pick versus the Jaguars. Just like that 2023 season we mentioned earlier, the issues have put the young quarterback in a dangerous downwards spiral. He knows it himself. “I think the ball starts rolling like that, we can’t get out of our own way — can’t get out of my own way, personally,” Maye said after the Jaguars game . “I have to look myself in the mirror and take this as a turning point. It’s Week 3, and at the same time we have to get some fuel and realize that what we’re doing out there offensively is unacceptable. It’s been unacceptable for three weeks. So, I have to start with myself and then lead these guys, and we have to get back after it.” Maye does seem to find some solace in the fact that the Patriots bounced back from a 1-2 start last season as well, but his head coach sang a different tune on Monday. “We’re not focused on last year. Each situation and each play is different,” said Mike Vrabel. For the Patriots, the situation is clear as day: if they can’t fix their quarterback, it’s game over for at least 2026. That fixing will not be easy, but also not impossible. As a starter, the Patriots have to get his confidence back up. Naturally, that is easier said than done, but amid all the disappointment through Week 3 there also have been glimpses. On Sunday, for example, Maye did throw some good passes. The drive that ended with his first interception down at the goal line? It was set up by a well-executed 38-yard pass connection with DeMario Douglas that was nearly followed up with another big gain out of a no-huddle look on the very first snap; Maye overshot Douglas — whether faulty ball placement or an imprecise route is to blame cannot be said at this point — but the play was there to be had. And maybe that is something the Patriots can use to get Maye back on track: no huddle. They did not use any up-tempo snaps in Weeks 1 and 2, partially due to game situation. Against Jacksonville, that incompletion was one of two no-huddle plays; the other being a 34-yard pass to Kyle Williams that could have become a 50-yard touchdown had the second-year wideout not stepped out of bounds. Ultimately, none of those moments helped tip the scales in New England’s favor versus the Jaguars. Neither did a 21-yard Maye touchdown run being brought back by penalty or the defense failing to get a single red zone stop. What those moments and multiple others throughout this so-far underwhelming season show, however, is that there is hope. Unlike 2023, when it became obvious that Mac Jones and Bailey Zappe were a lost cause in New England, Maye continues to have his moments of brilliance. The problem is that they are overshadowed by head-scratching decisions and insufficient ball security. But, and here is the glass-half-full-perspective, those issues can be fixed. Just ask the man himself. “It’s not that I feel like these mistakes that I’m making personally are really them beating us. I think it’s beating myself,” he said. “You have to flip to the next play and realize that this league will humble you quick. Just finding ways for me to step up when I feel like I’m not playing my best and still lead the team. I think that’s what this position is about, and that’s what as the quarterback of this football team is my obligation.” Drake Maye looks broken right now and the buttons he is pushing are not functioning properly, there is no sugar-coating it. However, he also is not beyond salvaging either.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Are the Saints actually a couple bad calls away from being 3-0?
summary: The New Orleans Saints are 1-2 after three weeks, but is it true they are a few officiating decisions away from being 3-0? That is the latest overreaction worth exploring after another frustrating loss. New Orleans has now been on the wrong side of controversial calls in both of its losses this season. The latest […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are 1-2 after three weeks, but is it true they are a few officiating decisions away from being 3-0? That is the latest overreaction worth exploring after another frustrating loss. New Orleans has now been on the wrong side of controversial calls in both of its losses this season. The latest came Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders, when a fourth-quarter sack-fumble by Tyler Shough was upheld on replay, while the Raiders got three extra chances to punch the ball in the endzone due to questionable penalties. That does not necessarily make the officiating the reason New Orleans lost either game. It does, however, make the Saints’ 1-2 record more interesting. Against Detroit, New Orleans had opportunities to win despite the controversial ruling. The same was true against Las Vegas. The Saints led the Raiders 27-16 in the second half and appeared to be in control before everything unraveled. New Orleans turned the ball over on all four of its fourth-quarter possessions, including two lost fumbles and an interception. Las Vegas turned those mistakes into points and rallied for a 35-27 victory. That is where the “couple bad calls away from 3-0” argument becomes complicated. There is no denying that officiating has been a major storyline in the Saints’ two losses. But New Orleans has also had chances to put those games away and failed to do so. Sunday was the clearest example. The Saints’ offense was extremely efficient for most of the afternoon. Shough threw four touchdown passes, Chris Olave had nine catches for 107 yards, and New Orleans converted 9-of-15 third downs while going 4-for-4 in the red zone. Yet they couldn’t finish the game with a win. So, yes, the Saints could reasonably argue that officiating has affected their record. But saying they’re simply 3-0 without the poor officiating would ignore the opportunities they’ve had to win these games themselves. And perhaps that’s what makes this an interesting overreaction. New Orleans may not be as far away from a 3-0 start as its record suggests. But the Saints still have to prove they can finish games when the opportunity is there.
author: Nic Jennings

title: State of the NFC South: Week 3 recap
summary: Just when you think you know how the division is going, almost nothing goes as everyone expected. Tampa Bay Buccaneers It’s not crazy to say that Bucs HC Todd Bowles could be fired after Week 4. This team has been one of the biggest disappointments in the NFL, and their performance against the Minnesota Vikings […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints warms up before kickoff against the Las Vegas Raiders prior to the NFL football game atCesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just when you think you know how the division is going, almost nothing goes as everyone expected. Tampa Bay Buccaneers It’s not crazy to say that Bucs HC Todd Bowles could be fired after Week 4. This team has been one of the biggest disappointments in the NFL, and their performance against the Minnesota Vikings was bad. The score showed a 7-point game in the end, but the Bucs made mistakes, and Baker Mayfield struggled. Speaking of Mayfield, near the end of the game, he injured his finger, which looked really bad. Next week, the Bucs play the Packers, so they could win, but it’s doubtful. Carolina Panthers Speaking of shock, the Panthers lost to the Cleveland Browns. First thing, this means the Browns are 2-0 against the NFC South so far. May spell bad news for the rest of the division, but going away from that, let’s focus on this game. The Panthers’ defense didn’t do enough against a Browns offense they should have handled. It doesn’t help that star CB Jaycee Horn went down with an injury and will be out for most of the season. The offense was also very disappointing and looked nothing like their first two weeks. A performance to forget. Atlanta Falcons Somehow, the Falcons are the only winners of the week. After Michael Penix returned, all eyes were on their QB situation, and he did well in his first game. The real hero was Bijan Robinson, who completely controlled this game for Atlanta and gave the Packers zero chance of winning. Could this win be the Packers just being a mess? I actually don’t think so. If Atlanta won by 3 points, then I would say that’s the case, but the Falcons won 35-14. We are going to see up close what this Falcons team really is, because Atlanta is playing the Saints this week. New Orleans Saints And now, a rant I have been waiting for. The Saints’ loss to the Raiders was one of the most frustrating losses since the Drew Brees/Sean Payton era. This game should have been won by New Orleans, and that fourth-quarter collapse was embarrassing. It was really one of the first times the Saints faced adversity while winning, and just like the Ravens last week, they couldn’t recover. The refs had a hand in making that happen, and some of those calls/no calls were truly mind-boggling, but this team had chances to overcome these, and they couldn’t. It sucks for everyone because I do think many of the Saints’ early weaknesses were fixed in this game. The run game was much better, Taliese Fuaga’s blocking improved, the Saints started fast, the run defense played really well, and the playcalling was exceptional at times. Momentum is a killer, and the Saints fell victim to it. Travis Etienne’s injury is extremely worrying, and the Saints must bring in an RB ahead of this week’s game, but I also think the pass rush needs more talent. This defense had its worst game so far in 2026, and the pass rush behind Chase Young was completely missing. The Saints won’t be able to survive with these two units where they are right now. NFC South standings: Carolina Panthers (1-2) New Orleans Saints (1-2) Atlanta Falcons (1-2) Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-3)
author: Caleb Yaccarino

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Raiders
summary: The Good: Tyler Shough The Saints quarterback threw 4 touchdowns for the first time in his career on Sunday and continued his strong start to the season against the Raiders. Shough found tight ends Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant twice each in the end zone and found Chris Olave nine times for 107 yards. Shough […]
full_text: The Good: Tyler Shough The Saints quarterback threw 4 touchdowns for the first time in his career on Sunday and continued his strong start to the season against the Raiders. Shough found tight ends Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant twice each in the end zone and found Chris Olave nine times for 107 yards. Shough did throw a costly interception in the 4th quarter but up until that point he had played a great game. The offensive line started to get beat in the fourth quarter which also led to a “fumble” by Shough which started the comeback for Vegas, but all things considered the Saints QB was not the biggest reason this game went awry in the fourth quarter and overall had a pretty good game. The Bad: Pass Defense The Saints allowed Raiders QB Kirk Cousins to complete 22/33 passes for 248 yards and 3 TDs with no interceptions. Brock Bowers returned for Las Vegas and had an immediate impact catching 10 passes for 116 yards and a touchdown. Chase Young had two sacks, but outside of Young no one on the Saints has been able to consistently put pressure on the QB this year, as no one else on the team has more than 1 sack so far. The defense couldn’t get the stops they needed to at the end of the game, as after taking a 27-16 lead the Saints allowed 19 straight points to the Raiders on three drives which all lasted just 6 or fewer plays. The Ugly: Turnovers The last four drives of the day for the Saints all ended in turnovers, three of which were fumbles and one interception. Shough fumbled twice, but the offensive line did not do him any favors on either and also got beat on the interception he threw. The first fumble came on a play that looked more like a forward pass than the one called back in Detroit in Week 1. The NFL is going to have to explain in detail the difference between the two plays, as right now it looks like their rules are not being enforced consistently by their officiating crews. The bad call by the refs completely derailed the game, as instead of potentially going up two scores the Saints fell behind thanks to the officials ruling the Shough play a fumble. Call it a fumble if you want, but if that was a fumble than so was the play in Detroit, and all we want is a little consistency and also some accountability if the refs miss a call that potentially changes the outcome of a game. The refs were not the sole reason or even the biggest reason the Saints lost however, as the offensive line was completely overwhelmed in the fourth quarter. There are many things that were ugly about this game, but the ultimate result of them was the Saints just giving the ball back to the Raiders when they had multiple chances to take the lead or tie in the final frame. The offensive line could be a problem going forward without Kelvin Banks Jr., but hopefully they will get it figured out as the Falcons come to town off their first win in a Monday night showdown next week.
author: Hayden Reel

title: Saints RB Travis Etienne Jr. expected to miss time due to hamstring injury
summary: It seems that Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara will have to take control of the rushing attack for the foreseeable future, as leading rusher Travis Etienne Jr. will likely miss time with a hamstring injury. Saints head coach Kellen Moore met with the media today and gave an update regarding Etienne Jr., stating that he […]
full_text: It seems that Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara will have to take control of the rushing attack for the foreseeable future, as leading rusher Travis Etienne Jr. will likely miss time with a hamstring injury. Saints head coach Kellen Moore met with the media today and gave an update regarding Etienne Jr., stating that he is expected to have “time lost.” Moore went on to say, “We’ll see ultimately what that timeline looks like. It’s just an unfortunate thing.” Etienne was working through a hamstring issue in the same leg throughout last week. The injury occurred in the third quarter when Etienne broke off a 16-yard run to the right side. As he was running down the sideline, he slowed down, reached for the back of his left leg, and took a hard hit out of bounds. That would ultimately be his final appearance in the game. Etienne was a vital offseason acquisition for the Saints, especially with the team’s need to elevate its rushing attack. Now, the run game falls squarely on the shoulders of Miller and Kamara as the Saints prepare for a Monday night matchup against the Falcons in the Dome.
author: Anthony Parker

title: Game Recap: Saints host Raiders in home opener
summary: The New Orleans Saints at last played their home opener when they hosted the Las Vegas Raiders in the late window on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a look back at all that went down in the Caesars Superdome. First Quarter The hosts received the opening kickoff but went three-and-out. The Raiders, meanwhile, found instant momentum as […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints stretches for a first down as Isaiah Pola-Mao #20 of the Las Vegas Raiders makes the tackle during the fourth quarter at Caesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints at last played their home opener when they hosted the Las Vegas Raiders in the late window on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a look back at all that went down in the Caesars Superdome. First Quarter The hosts received the opening kickoff but went three-and-out. The Raiders, meanwhile, found instant momentum as Kirk Cousins completed his first four throws for 53 yards, including three receptions by tight end Brock Bowers who was suiting up for the first time this season. But after an offensive holding and a sack by Chase Young, the defense was able to hold Vegas to a field goal attempt. Matt Gay converted from 41 yards. The Saints faced another quick three-and-out as they began their ensuing series, but a huge 3rd down scramble from Tyler Shough for 36 yards kicked the offense into life. Travis Etienne Jr had some work on the ground, and Shough found Devaughn Vele and Chris Olave for double-digit gains as the Saints entered the red zone. CJ Donaldson would then run for 5 yards to set up a 2-yard touchdown throw from Shough to Juwan Johnson. Daniel Carlson’s extra point was blocked by his former team, so the score remained 6-3. Second Quarter The Raiders began their next drive at the 40 after the kickoff fell short of the landing zone. They drove past midfield with a run from Mike Washington, before Cousins found Michael Mayer for 18 yards. An offside penalty helped the defensive effort as the Saints were able to force another field goal attempt, which Gay converted from 37 yards to tie the game at 6-6. New Orleans then went three-and-out, and punted to the visitors who began the ensuing possession at midfield. The Raiders took full advantage, with Cousins continuing to find Mayer and Bowers as they entered the red zone. The Saints thought they’d done enough to keep Vegas out of the end zone again, but a roughing the passer penalty against Danny Stutsman for what looked like a perfect hit on the quarterback gave the Raiders 1st-and-goal. Cousins found Mayer for the 3-yard score, and the visitors took a 13-6 lead. Etienne had a few short gains on the ground to begin the Saints’ next possession, before Shough found Olave twice in a row for a total of 29 yards. He then found his tight ends Noah Fant and Johnson, before another short run from Etienne put the ball at the 3-yard line. Shough found Fant in the end zone for the score, and Carlson’s extra point levelled the game at 13-13. Cousins ran a successful two-minute drill before the half, helped by another pair of big gains through Bowers. A 25-yard field goal from Gay gave Vegas a 16-13 lead as time expired. Third Quarter The Raiders went three-and-out to begin the second half. Shough continued to have success moving the football as he returned to the field, with passes to Vele and Etienne alongside runs from Alvin Kamara moving the black and gold past midfield. Shough continued to sling it, connecting with Johnson, Vele, and Olave to move the hosts to the 1-yard line. It was Johnson again who caught another touchdown pass, continuing the game of the tight-ends. Trailing 20-16, the Raiders return-man Dylan Laube then fumbled the kickoff return. The Saints recovered, and took instant advantage. Etienne broke out a 16-yard run before Shough threw to Fant for a 16-yard touchdown pass, and just like that the hosts were up 27-16. But the Raiders did well to respond, as Bowers continued his dominant display with a 20-yard catch to move the drive past midfield. Before long, Washington ran in a 36-yard touchdown to cut into the lead. After an unsuccessful 2-point conversion attempt, the score remained 27-22. The team exchanged quick punts after that, before an 11-yard pass from Shough to Olave on 3rd down extended the ensuing series for the black and gold and put them into Vegas territory. Fourth Quarter Shough converted another 3rd down to Olave a few plays later. But with the Saints on the edge of field goal range, Shough was sacked and stripped by Malcolm Koonce as he intended to throw, in the same fashion that Chase Young got to Jared Goff in Week 1. The fumble was recovered by the defense, but this time, the ruling on the field stood and Vegas would take over. Cousins found Ashton Jeanty for 22 yards to begin the drive, before connecting with Tre Tucker for 15 yards a few plays later. Cody White would catch the short touchdown to restore the lead for the visitors. After another failed 2-point conversion, they led just 28-27. But the Saints’ woes would then continue as Shough’s pass for Bryce Lance was picked off by Hezekiah Masses. Masses then fumbled himself, but the Raiders fell on it again and had 1st-and-goal from the 4-yard line. The Saints stopped Jeanty twice before on 3rd down Cousins connected with Bowers in the end zone, and the Raiders went up 35-27. Still just a one-score game, the Saints did promptly enter the red zone helped by runs from Kamara and a 22-yard throw to Johnson. But Shough fumbled as he was sacked again, with Maxx Crosby forcing the ball out. The defense forced the Raiders into a quick punt to keep hopes alive. But in the two-minute drill, Johnson fumbled after a catch near midfield as turnovers continued to mount for the black and gold. The Raiders jumped on it, and knelt out the clock from there to secure a 35-27 win. The Saints’ focus now turns to Monday Night Football when they host the Atlanta Falcons in a week’s time.
author: Sam Mackenzie

title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Raiders
summary: The New Orleans Saints fell to 1-2 after a fourth-quarter meltdown to the Las Vegas Raiders, allowing 19 unanswered points. While the Saints looked to have finally fixed their slow starts, other problems arose, and there are more questions than answers. Up: RB Travis Etienne Jr. Through the first two weeks of the regular season, […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Ashton Jeanty #2 of the Las Vegas Raiders is tackled by Kool-Aid McKinstry #1 of the New Orleans Saints during the second quarter at Caesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints fell to 1-2 after a fourth-quarter meltdown to the Las Vegas Raiders, allowing 19 unanswered points. While the Saints looked to have finally fixed their slow starts, other problems arose, and there are more questions than answers. Up: RB Travis Etienne Jr. Through the first two weeks of the regular season, the Saints haven’t seen the production match the large contract they gave running back Travis Etienne Jr. The fifth-year running back signed a $48 million deal in the offseason and headlined the New Orleans’ expensive running game rebuild. Fortunately for the Saints, Etienne finally started to find consistency as a runner during their home opener against the Raiders. Unfortunately for New Orleans, Etienne would leave the game in the third quarter and not return. Etienne ended the day with 13 carries for 57 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry. The Saints entered the day with a clear game plan: get Etienne involved. He was a valuable part of the team’s first-half scoring drives and was on his way to having his best day as a Saint. But after Etienne left, the wind was taken out of the Saints’ sails, and it was clear he was pivotal to their game plan. Up: DE Chase Young Defensive end Chase Young continues his strong season, following his 1.5-sack game with 2 sacks on Sunday. Young ended the day with 2 tackles, 2 sacks, and 2 tackles for loss. Young is a game wrecker. Opposing offenses are accounting for him on every down, and he creates chaos when rushing the passer. The eighth-year pass rusher is finally blossoming into the star he was projected to be when he was drafted second overall, and you can look for him to make a play when the Saints need him the most. While the rest of the Saints’ defense struggled during Sunday’s loss, Young came out with a strong showing. Down: Magical Fourth Quarter We’ve spent all week analyzing the Saints’ slow starts and monster fourth quarters, exclaiming, “If only they could play in the first half how they play in the fourth quarter.” Well, we finally saw the Saints’ start significantly quicker, finding the end zone twice and scoring 13 points in the first half, compared to just 6 over their first two games. While the Saints finally found the answers to scoring in the first half, they suffered a complete meltdown in the fourth quarter, turning the ball over four times and allowing 13 points. The Saints’ monster fourth quarters weren’t going to last forever, but the meltdown was a complete counter to the strong showings we’ve seen in the past weeks. Simply put, if New Orleans was even 20% as good as they’ve been in the fourth quarter this season on Sunday, they would’ve come out with the win. The loss falls mainly on the offenses’ inability to protect the ball and run the clock. Down: Defense By far the biggest standout from Sunday’s loss was the defense’s inability to stop the Raiders from scoring. Las Vegas started the game scoring on each of their first four drives, and scored on 7 of their 11 offensive drives. The Raiders established early on that they wanted to get superstar tight end Brock Bowers the ball, and the Saints failed to successfully counter it. New Orleans even assigned their best cornerback, Kool-Aid McKinstry, to mirror Bowers, but he still came away with 10 receptions for 116 yards and a touchdown. It also appeared the Saints defense was too content after going up 27-16, with the following drive being too easy and efficient for the Raiders offense. After New Orleans scored a touchdown to go up 11, the defense allowed a five-play, 71-yard drive. The Saints defense was the backbone of the team during their rebuilding season last year, with defensive coordinator Brandon Staley’s name lingering around a possible head coaching return. But over the first three weeks of the season, New Orleans is allowing 27 points per game.
author: Kyle Besson

title: Saints vs. Falcons odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
summary: The New Orleans Saints are now 1-2 after falling to the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday night at the Caesars Superdome in a game that featured what was another very controversial call by the officials. The call came in the fourth quarter when Raiders defensive end Malcolm Koonce hit Tyler Shough as he attempted to […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JANUARY 04: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints rushes against Kaden Elliss #55 of the Atlanta Falcons during the second half of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are now 1-2 after falling to the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday night at the Caesars Superdome in a game that featured what was another very controversial call by the officials. The call came in the fourth quarter when Raiders defensive end Malcolm Koonce hit Tyler Shough as he attempted to throw. The officials ruled that Shough lost control of the ball before his hand began moving forward, making it a fumble rather than an incomplete pass. The ruling was upheld after review, giving Las Vegas possession and adding another frustrating chapter in the book of discrepancies from NFL officiating. Unfortunately, that fumble became the turning point of the game as the Saints were leading 27-22 and we’re at Raiders’ 30-yard line with a chance to extend their lead when Shough lost the ball. Instead, the Raiders were given possession and scored shortly after to take a 28-27 lead. The turnover resulted in a complete shift in momentum for the Saints, becoming the first of four straight possessions to end in turnovers as the Raiders scored the final 19 points of the game. The Saints will look to bounce back this week in what will be an emotional matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The game will recognize the 20th anniversary of the historic “Domecoming” game, when New Orleans returned to the Superdome for the first time following the devastation of Hurricane Katrina. With one of the NFL’s biggest rivalries taking center stage, there is certainly no love lost between these two teams. Under the bright lights of Monday Night Football, with a national audience watching, both teams will have plenty to prove as they write the next chapter in their heated NFC South feud. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently 2.5-point favorites against the Falcons, with an over/under of 48.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. title: NY Giants QB J.J. McCarthy: Film shows lots of good … and bad
summary: The New York Giants traded a 2027 fifth-round pick for quarterback J.J. McCarthy on Monday. The 2024 10th overall selection missed his rookie season due to a torn right meniscus. He also missed five games in 2025 with a high ankle sprain and one game with a concussion.  The 6-foot-3, 219-pound 23-year-old signal caller threw […]
full_text: J.J. McCarthy | Getty Images The New York Giants traded a 2027 fifth-round pick for quarterback J.J. McCarthy on Monday. The 2024 10th overall selection missed his rookie season due to a torn right meniscus. He also missed five games in 2025 with a high ankle sprain and one game with a concussion. The 6-foot-3, 219-pound 23-year-old signal caller threw for 1,632 yards with a 57.6% completion rate last season. He threw 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions, with a 7.3% big-time-throw rate and a 4.8% turnover-worthy play rate. The Vikings dropped 17 of his passes, and he rushed for 181 yards with four touchdowns and six fumbles. McCarthy was relegated to third string after the Vikings signed Kyler Murray and had Carson Wentz to the roster. What McCarthy offers McCarthy’s film was frustrating. There’s no denying his athletic ability and how his legs will be an asset in Matt Nagy’s scheme, but his mechanics, accuracy, and decision-making were maddening at times. McCarthy air-mailed several throws, threw awkwardly from clean pockets and made easy completions much harder than they had to be. His accuracy issues, though, could be attributed to wild mechanics. However, he had several WOW-type plays throughout his bad season, and his throws – when his footwork was correct – had improved accuracy. McCarthy showed impressive velocity throughout his tape. He ripped several far hash throws and there were plays where he navigated the pocket well and delivered good throws, while using his eyes well: via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY The play above against the Giants is an elite pass to Justin Jefferson (18) against tight coverage. There was one place that the football could have been delivered to ensure that Jefferson caught the ball, and McCarthy delivered it. Below is another play-action rip that resulted in a touchdown: via GIPHY We see the heavy personnel, under-center, play-action use against Dallas. Plays like this – where McCarthy threw on the run off a bootleg – are plays that easily fit into what Nagy and Greg Roman will ask of McCarthy if/when he sees the field. I wish I could say, however, that McCarthy was generally accurate throwing on the run, but McCarthy had some very poor throws while on the move last season; we’ll see that later. McCarthy had a dim flash of touch passes throughout his tape, which was an issue of his at Michigan. His passes were delivered on a line too often, making the catch more difficult for the receivers. But plays like this one below, where McCarthy used touch, did pop up every now and again, which was encouraging: via GIPHY via GIPHY McCarthy is comfortable throwing over the middle of the field. Of throws inside the numbers of 20-air yards or less, McCarthy finished 31 of 59 ( 53% ) with a positive EPA. Again, he flashed high-level throws, carving through zone coverage while showcasing good arm talent, but these throws were coupled with good footwork; unfortunately, it wasn’t consistent throughout his tape, but here are some throws that highlight his ability to throw over the middle of the field: via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY Off play-action, McCarthy rips a pass to T.J. Hockenson (87). Watch how McCarthy steps into the pocket with trust and just delivers the concept after hitching up. This was an exceptional play by McCarthy. McCarthy again looked poised against Dallas, throwing this seam ball to Hockenson against bailing middle-hook zone defenders: via GIPHY McCarthy hit the receiver in stride on third down against a trailing man defender, just in front of the safety: via GIPHY Here’s another successful play against the Giants off play-action where McCarthy pump fakes to displace the Giants before delivering a completion to Jordan Addison (3). via GIPHY McCarthy also had several high-level back-shoulder throws away from defensive leverage. The play against the Giants was very impressive, for it was a back-shoulder toward the middle of the field with Dexter Lawrence (97) in his face, while the other two come from completely clean pockets: via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY McCarthy is a threat with his legs; he rushed for 894 yards through three seasons at Michigan, with an average of six yards per carry. He also averaged 3.07 yards after contact through college. He wasn’t used on a ton of designed rushes with Kevin O’Connell and the Vikings last year, but I expect that to change with the Giants. Here are a few quarterback scrambles that showcase his speed and movement skills: via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY Then there’s McCarthy’s ability to throw on the run; there were some good one, like these… via GIPHY via GIPHY Reasons for concern …Then there are plays with McCarthy on the move where he is wildly inaccurate: via GIPHY via GIPHY The mechanics and accuracy issues are married, and correctable, which is excellent for both McCarthy and the Giants, but it was certainly a problem in 2025 for the Vikings. via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY McCarthy also used suspect decision-making through the 2025 season. There were several plays where it seemed like he negligently forced the issue: via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY via GIPHY Final thoughts The Giants acquired a talented young quarterback with tools that MUST be ironed out. McCarthy is mobile, has good velocity, and has made high-level throws at the NFL level, but WOW, did he make mistakes throughout his 2025 season. That said, I believe the Giants can leverage his tools; his mobility will be an asset and will be used more often in Roman’s rush scheme, but McCarthy’s lower-body mechanics and decision-making must improve. This trade is a new start for McCarthy, and it gives the Giants an interesting insurance option behind Winston. I get it.

title: NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 4
summary: No. 1 — Buffalo Bills (1st) SAME Somehow, the Buffalo Bills turned the football over five times and still WON THE GAME! Of course, it was against the Chargers, who are currently — and historically — allergic to winning, but James Cook’s 154 yards on the ground helped give Buffalo the 24-16 win, and they […]
full_text: Brock Purdy | Getty Images No. 1 — Buffalo Bills (1st) SAME Somehow, the Buffalo Bills turned the football over five times and still WON THE GAME! Of course, it was against the Chargers, who are currently — and historically — allergic to winning, but James Cook’s 154 yards on the ground helped give Buffalo the 24-16 win, and they remain at the top of the standings here. No. 2 — San Francisco 49ers (5th) 📈 3 spots Brock Purdy and the 49ers are one of the hottest teams in football. Purdy went for 297 yards and four touchdowns against an inferior Cardinals team, who pushed the 49ers in the 36-30 game. Still, through all the injuries, the 49ers remain a top team in the NFL. No. 3 — Kansas City Chiefs (7th) 📈 3 spots The Chiefs went into Miami and easily handled the Dolphins. Patrick Mahomes was efficient (20 of 24 for 246 yards with two touchdowns), and Rashee Rice finally got going with seven catches for 88 yards. Miami offered little resistance in the 24-10 win, and the Chiefs are one of the four undefeated teams that remain in the NFL. No. 4 — Seattle Seahawks (2nd) 📉 2 spots Seattle goy Sam Darnold back from his hip injury, but Washington did an excellent job harrassing the Seahawks all game. Darnold finished with 379 passing yards and four touchdowns, but Marcus Mariota did enough to give the Commanders a 33-31 home victory. No. 5 — Los Angeles Rams (3rd) 📉 2 spots The Rams drop to 1-2 but remain in the top five. Massive credit to the Broncos, who appeared dead for much of the game but battled back with 30 second-half points. Matt Stafford finished with 390 yards passing and two touchdowns, but the Rams’ game plan shifted after a Terrance Ferguson injury, and they were without Puka Nukua, who they hope will return soon. No. 6 — Baltimore Ravens (7th) 📈 2 spots Tyler Loop! The Ravens and Dallas were headed to overtime after Dak Prescott led the Cowboys down the field on a last-minute drive to tie the game with a field goal. Unfortunately for Dallas, Lamar Jackson found Zay Flowers for 27 yards, which set up a 56-yarder from Loop for a big road victory over Jerry Jones’ Cowboys. No. 7 — Minnesota Vikings (11th) 📈 4 spots The Vikings have moved eight spots up in the rankings over the last two weeks. They’re undefeated, but sit seventh in the rankings; this is because of my discomfort with Kyler Murray, who missed Week 2 with a concussion. The Vikings’ defense, led by Brian Flores, is playing amazing football, and they beat up on the Buccaneers, 23-16. Still, the offense isn’t going to be bailed out by the strong defense every week; the team must become more complementary. No. 8 — Denver Broncos (14th) 📈 2 spots The Broncos defeated a very good Rams team at home with second-half resilience. The win was similar to their win over the Giants last year, where they scored 30 points in the fourth quarter; they did that in the second half, and the Broncos’ defense slowed down Matt Stafford when it mattered most. No. 9 — Chicago Bears (12th) 📈 3 spots Chicago dismantled the Philadelphia Eagles with 38-year -old journeyman quarterback Case Keenum. Ben Johnson continues to prove why he’s an offensive wizard, and he unlocked the potential of Luther Burden III in the game. Kalif Raymond finished with six grabs for 90 yards and a touchdown, as Philadelphia was held to seven points and 248 total yards. Impressive win against a struggling, now 2-1 Eagles team. No. 10 — Cincinnati Bengals (4th) 📉 6 spots The Bengals gave up 292 yards and three touchdowns to Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers. After two strong weeks of defensive football, the Bengals’ defense struggled to stop Ja’Marr Chase (9 catches for 98 yards and a touchdown) and Jaylen Warren, who rushed for 127 yards. Cincinnati will be okay, but this was a tough loss. No. 11 — Jacksonville Jaguars (13th) 📈 2 spots The New England Patriots are spiraling right now, and Jacksonville took advantage of that fact in Week 3. Jacksonville beat up on the Patriots, 35-6, with Drake Maye looking very bad, finishing 14 of 25 for 199 yards with a pair of interceptions. Jacksonville got back on track against the AFC champs from last season. No. 12 — Detroit Lions (15th) 📈 4 spots Detroit was pushed by the New York Jets, but they found a way to win late in the 31-24 game against a feisty Jets team. Jaymeir Gibbs finished with 99 yards and a pair of touchdowns on 20 carries, and the Lions sit at 2-1. No. 13 — Philadelphia Eagles (9th) 📉 4 spots The Eagles are a 2-1 team that does not inspire much hope. Jalen Hurts still has his flaws as a passer, and they were just embarrassed in primetime by the Chicago Bears. Things do not get much easier for the Eagles, as they host the Rams next Sunday and then travel to London to play the Jaguars. No. 14 — Las Vegas Raiders (24th) 📈 10 spots The Raiders are undefeated! And they just went into a hostile New Orleans environment and defeated the Saints 35-21. Brock Bowers’ return was exciting, as the young tight end caught 10 passes for 116 yards and a touchdown. Kirk Cousins is doing enough to put the Raiders into advantageous situations, as they sit undefeated. No. 15 — Dallas Cowboys (14th) 📉 1 spot I hate having the 1-2 Dallas Cowboys this high, especially with their suspect defense through three weeks. But I know how explosive their offense can be with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Plus, their rushing attack is getting going, and they’ll be getting Tyler Smith back soon. The defense remains an issue, of course, but Dallas stays put at 14. No. 16 — Pittsburgh Steelers (22nd) 📈 5 spots I didn’t expect to see Aaron Rodgers dial back the clock against a Bengals defense that tormented the Buccaneers and Texans in their first two matchups. The Steelers’ defense remains their strength, but competent quarterback play makes them a threat, so they are in the top-fifteen. No. 17 — Indianapolis Colts (20th) 📈 3 spots The Colts finally got their first victory against the Houston Texans on a last-second field goal. Indianapolis struggled to do much against a very good Texans defense, but they found a way to get a valuable win and send the Texans to 0-3. No. 18 — Houston Texans (17th) 📉 1 spot I don’t like having the 0-3 Texans this high, but I feel better about their position — specifically with their defense — than I do with the remaining teams, including the injured Giants, so here we are. Houston pushed Buffalo and the Colts to near victories; they must get more out of their offense and learn to secure wins, but they’re better than their 0-3 record would indicate. No. 19 — New York Giants (21st) 📈 2 spots The Giants are 2-1 and handled their business in a sloppy noreaster against the Tennessee Titans. New York has issues with Jameis Winston; the trade for J.J. McCarthy may eventually solve that problem, but the Giants are beat up on both sides of the ball. However, Jordan Stout is a stud. The Giants can still compete for this NFC East with their current injury situation, and I expect better play out of Jameis Winston, although I’m relieved they’ll have another viable option. No. 20 — Washington Commanders (26th) 📈 6 spots Washington pulled off one of the season’s more impressive wins, defeating the Super Bowl champions 33-31 at home. Perhaps it was Sam Darnold jitters, or the dreaded one-o-clock start for a West Coast team — I’m not sure — but it does seem like Washington’s defense has improved, and Marcus Mariota did enough against Mike Macdonald’s talented defense No. 21 — New Orleans Saints (18th)📉 3 spots Las Vegas just might be a much better football team than many anticipated, and the Saints found that out firsthand. Tyler Shough played well, throwing four touchdowns with 255 yards passing. Still, the Raiders forced four turnovers and the Saints lost running back Travis Etienne to injury. New Orleans is a quality 1-2 team, but they’re still young and learning themselves. No. 22 — Carolina Panthers (20th) 📉 2 spots The Panthers suffered a tough loss to the now 2-1 Browns. Bryce…
